title: Various events from the same counsel
paragraphs: Jacques Amyot, grand almoner of France, one day told me a story that does great honour to one of our princes — and ours he was on several very good counts, though originally of foreign extraction. During our first commotions, at the siege of Rouen, this prince was warned by the queen-mother of a conspiracy against his life, with her letters naming the very man who was to carry it out: a gentleman of Anjou or Maine who normally frequented the prince's household. The prince did not breathe a syllable of this to anyone. The next day he went up to St Catherine's Mount, from which our battery was playing against the town (for the siege was still on), accompanied by the said lord almoner and another bishop. He saw the gentleman who had been pointed out to him, and sent for him at once. When the man came before him, already pale and trembling under the weight of his guilt, the prince said: "Monsieur So-and-so, you can guess what I have to say to you; your face gives it away. There's no point in disguising your scheme — I'm so well informed of your business that any attempt to conceal or deny it will only make things worse for you. You know perfectly well such-and-such details" (the most secret circumstances of the conspiracy), "so as you value your life, confess the whole truth of the plot." The poor man, seeing himself trapped and convicted (the whole business had been disclosed to the queen by one of the accomplices), didn't know what to do. He folded his hands, begged and pleaded for mercy, and threw himself at his prince's feet. The prince raised him up and went on: "Now, sir, tell me — have I ever offended you? Have I, out of private hatred or malice, wronged any kinsman or friend of yours? It's not even three weeks since I first laid eyes on you. What could possibly have driven you to attempt my death?" In a trembling voice the gentleman replied that it was no private grudge against him personally, but the general interest of his party; that certain people had urged him on, persuading him it would be a meritorious act, by any means available, to wipe out so great and so powerful an enemy of their religion. "Well," said the prince, "I'll show you how much more charitable my religion is than yours. Yours has counselled you to kill me, without hearing me speak, without my having given you any cause for offence; mine commands me to forgive you, even though by your own confession you stand convicted of a design to kill me without reason. Get out. Don't let me see you again. And if you're wise, choose more honest counsellors from now on for your schemes."

The Emperor Augustus, while in Gaul, received reliable information of a conspiracy that L. Cinna was contriving against him. He resolved to make an example of the man, and to that end summoned his friends to meet in council the next morning. But the intervening night he spent in great inner agitation, considering that he was about to put to death a young man from an illustrious family, nephew to the great Pompey. The thought drove him into a series of passionate outbursts. "What then," he said, "am I to live in perpetual anxiety and alarm, and let my would-be assassin wander freely about? Will he go unpunished for having conspired against my life — a life I've defended through so many civil wars, so many battles by land and sea? After settling universal peace over the whole world, am I to pardon a man who's plotted not just to murder me but to slaughter me at sacrifice?" — for the plan was to kill him while he officiated. After a long silence he started up again, louder, raging at himself: "Why are you alive, if so many would benefit from your death? Will there be no end to your reprisals and cruelties? Is your life worth so much that so much harm must be done to preserve it?" His wife Livia, seeing him in this perplexity, said: "Will you take a woman's advice? Do as the physicians do — when the usual remedies fail, try the opposite. Severity has got you nowhere so far: Lepidus followed Salvidienus, Murena followed Lepidus, Caepio followed Murena, Egnatius followed Caepio. Try sweetness and clemency now. Cinna is convicted; pardon him. He'll never have the heart to harm you afterwards, and it'll add to your glory." Augustus was relieved to find an advocate of his own inclination. He thanked his wife, countermanded the summons to council, and ordered Cinna to be brought to him alone. When Cinna arrived, the room cleared and a chair set for him, Augustus said: "First, Cinna, I ask you to hear me out patiently. Don't interrupt — I'll give you time to answer afterwards. You know, Cinna, that I took you prisoner in the enemy's camp, where you were not merely an enemy by circumstance but an enemy by birth. I spared your life, restored all your goods, and finally set you up so comfortably by my generosity that the victors envied the defeated. The priestly office you petitioned me for, I granted you — after denying it to others whose fathers had always borne arms in my service. After all these favours, you've undertaken to kill me." Cinna cried out that he was very far from harbouring any such wicked thought. "You're not keeping your promise, Cinna," Augustus continued, "that you wouldn't interrupt me. Yes, you've undertaken to murder me, in such a place, on such a day, in such company, in such a manner." At those words, seeing Cinna struck dumb — not because of his promise but because his conscience had collapsed under the weight of the evidence — Augustus went on: "Now, to what end were you going to do it? To be emperor? Believe me, the Republic is in a sorry state if I'm the only man standing between you and the empire. You can't even defend your own household — only the other day you were beaten in a lawsuit by a mere freed slave's interest. Have you no means, no power anywhere except enough to take on Caesar? I'll step down from the throne if I'm the only obstacle to your hopes. Do you think the Paulli, the Fabii, the Cossii, the Servilii, and so many other noble Romans — noble not just in name but by the virtue that honours their nobility — would tolerate you?" After this, and a great deal more (he spoke for two long hours), he ended: "Now go, Cinna. Go. I give you the life I'd already given you once, when you were an enemy — and now I give it back to you again, traitor and parricide as you are. Let friendship begin between us from this moment, and let's see whether I have given, or you have received, your life with the better faith." And with that he left him. Some time later he advanced Cinna to the consulship, complaining that Cinna hadn't had the nerve to ask for it. He kept him afterwards as a very close friend, and was eventually made sole heir to his entire estate. Now — from the time of this episode, which befell Augustus in the fortieth year of his life, he never had another conspiracy or attempt made against him. He reaped the proper reward of his generous clemency. But things didn't go that way with our prince. His moderation and mercy did not protect him; he later fell into the net of a similar treason. So vain and futile a thing is human prudence; through all our projects, counsels, and precautions, Fortune will still be mistress of events.

We call physicians fortunate when they hit upon a lucky cure — as if theirs were the only art that couldn't stand on its own legs, whose foundations were too weak to support themselves, and as if no other art needed Fortune's hand to help it. For my part I think of medicine as much good or ill as anyone could want me to, since, thank God, we have no traffic with each other. I'm of the opposite humour to other men: I generally despise it; but when I'm sick, instead of recanting and coming to terms with it, I start to hate and fear it even more. I tell those who urge me to take medicine that they must at least give me time to recover my strength and health so I can better withstand the violence and danger of their potions. I let nature work, supposing her sufficiently armed with teeth and claws to defend herself against the assaults of illness and to uphold that structure whose dissolution she dreads. My fear is that, instead of helping her where she's grappling with disease, I'd be assisting her opponent and only piling more work on her.
Now, I say that not only in medicine but in other more reliable arts, Fortune has a very great share.

The poetic raptures, the flights of fancy that ravish and carry the author out of himself — why shouldn't we attribute them to his good fortune, since he himself admits they exceed his own capacity and force, acknowledging that they come from something other than himself, and that he has them no more in his power than orators say they have those extraordinary surges that sometimes push them beyond their own design? It's the same in painting, where strokes will sometimes slip from the painter's hand so far beyond his intention and his skill that they astonish even him. But Fortune shows her share in such things even more plainly through the graces and elegances we find in them — beyond, sometimes even without, the workman's awareness. A competent reader often discovers in another's writing perfections the author himself never intended or noticed, a richer sense and a more striking turn of phrase.

As for military enterprises, anyone can see how great a hand Fortune has in them. Even in our deliberations and counsels there must surely be something of chance and good luck mixed in with human prudence; for what wisdom can do on its own is no great matter. The keener, quicker, and more apprehensive it is, the more weakness it discovers in itself, and the more apt it is to distrust itself. I'm of Sulla's opinion; and when I look closely at the most glorious feats of war, it seems to me that those who conduct them use counsel and debate only for form's sake, leaving the best part of the enterprise to Fortune, and, leaning on her, breaking at every turn the bounds of military doctrine and the rules of war. There happen sometimes, in their deliberations, fortuitous bursts of energy and strange furies that mostly drive them to follow the worst-grounded plans, and swell their courage beyond reason's limits. That's why several of the great captains of old, to justify these rash resolutions, were obliged to tell their soldiers that some inspiration, some sign or omen, had invited them to the attempt.

So, in this doubt and uncertainty — in the short-sightedness of human wisdom that struggles to see and choose what's best because of the difficulties carried in by the various circumstances of things — the surest way, in my view, even without any other consideration urging us to it, is to pitch upon whatever has the greatest appearance of honesty and justice. If we can't be certain of the shortest road, let's keep to the straightest and most direct one. In the two examples I just gave, there's no question that it was nobler and more generous in the man who had received the offence to pardon it than to do otherwise. If the first miscarried for it, he's not to be blamed for his good intention; nor do we know whether, by acting otherwise, he'd have escaped the end his destiny had appointed him — and he'd at least have lost the glory of so humane an act.

You'll read in history of many who, fearing for their lives, took the course of meeting and pre-empting conspiracies by punishment and revenge; but I find very few who got any advantage from this — witness so many Roman emperors. Whoever finds himself in such danger ought not to expect much from his vigilance or his power. For how hard a thing it is to secure oneself from an enemy hiding behind the face of the most devoted friend, or to read the wills and inner thoughts of those in our personal service. It does little good to have a guard of foreigners around you and to be always fenced in by armed men: whoever despises his own life is master of yours. And besides, this continual suspicion, which makes a prince mistrustful of all the world, must of necessity be a strange torment to him. That's why Dion, when warned that Callippus was watching for an opportunity to take his life, never had the heart to inquire more closely into it. He said he'd rather die than live in that misery — having to stand continually on guard, not just against his enemies but against his friends too. Alexander demonstrated the same point even more vividly and more roundly in action when, having been warned by a letter from Parmenio that his most beloved physician Philip had been bought with Darius' money to poison him, he handed Philip the letter to read and at the same moment drank off the potion Philip had brought him. Wasn't this to express a resolution that if his friends meant to send him out of the world, he was willing to give them the opportunity? Alexander is the supreme model for daring acts; but I don't know whether there's another passage in his life that shows such firm courage as this, or so illustrious an image of the beauty and greatness of his mind.

Those who preach to princes such circumspect and vigilant jealousy and distrust in the name of security are preaching them ruin and dishonour. Nothing noble can be performed without danger. I know a man, naturally very daring and enterprising, whose good fortune is constantly spoiled by such persuasions — that he must keep himself closely surrounded by friends, must not listen to any reconciliation with old enemies, must hold himself aloof and never trust himself in hands stronger than his own, whatever promises or offers they may make, whatever advantages he may see in front of him. And I know another who has unexpectedly built his fortune by following the directly opposite advice.

Courage, whose reputation and glory men chase with such hungry appetite, presents itself when needed as magnificently in plain clothes as in full armour, in a private room as in a camp, with arms hanging down as with arms raised.

This over-cautious, over-wary prudence is a mortal enemy to all high and generous exploits. Scipio, in order to sound out Syphax's intentions, left his army, abandoned Spain — not yet secure or well settled in his new conquest — and crossed over into Africa in two small ships, to commit himself in an enemy country to the power of a barbarian king, on a faith untested and unknown, without any pledge, without hostages, on the sole security of the greatness of his own courage, his good fortune, and the promise of his high hopes.
"Habita fides ipsam plerumque fidem obligat."
["Trust often obliges fidelity." — Livy, xxii. 22.]

In a life of ambition and glory, you have to hold a tight rein on suspicion. Fear and distrust invite and draw on offence. The most mistrustful of our kings established his affairs chiefly by voluntarily putting his life and liberty into his enemies' hands — that act showing he had absolute confidence in them, so that they might place equal assurance in him. Caesar opposed only the authority of his face and the haughty sharpness of his rebukes to his mutinous legions in arms against him:
"Stetit aggere fulti Cespitis, intrepidus vultu: meruitque timeri, Nil metuens."
["He stood on a mound, his countenance intrepid, and earned the right to be feared, fearing nothing himself." — Lucan, v. 316.]

But it's also true that this undaunted assurance can't be represented in its full, pure form except by those whom the apprehension of death and the worst that can happen do not terrify. To go through the motions of a feigned resolution with a pale, doubtful face and trembling limbs, in service of some important reconciliation, will achieve nothing. It's an excellent way to win another's heart and goodwill, to submit and entrust oneself to him — provided it looks freely done, not forced by necessity, and in such a state that the man clearly does it out of complete confidence in the other party, or at least with a face untouched by any cloud of suspicion. When I was a boy I saw a gentleman, governor of a great city, who, faced with a popular uprising and fury and not knowing what else to do, walked out of a place of very great strength and safety to throw himself on the mercy of the seditious mob, hoping by that means to calm the tumult before it grew worse. It went badly for him: he was miserably killed there. Yet I don't think he committed so great a mistake in going out as people commonly reproach his memory with; his error was rather in choosing a gentle, submissive manner for his purpose, trying to quiet this storm by obeying rather than commanding, by entreaty rather than remonstrance. I'm inclined to think a gracious severity, with a soldierly way of issuing orders, full of confidence and authority appropriate to his rank and the dignity of his office, would have worked better for him — at any rate he'd have perished with more decency and reputation. There's nothing so impossible to expect from this many-headed monster in its fury as humanity and good nature; it is far more open to reverence and fear. I'd also reproach him that, having taken a resolution (brave rather than rash, in my judgment) to expose himself, weak and unprotected, on this tempestuous sea of raging madmen, he should have stuck to his role and not for an instant abandoned the lofty part he had undertaken. But once he saw the danger up close — and his nose happened to start bleeding — he switched the submissive, fawning expression he'd put on at first for one of fear and amazement, filled his voice with pleading and his eyes with tears, and tried to withdraw and save himself. That carriage only inflamed their fury, and soon brought its effects upon him.

On one occasion a general muster of several armed units was planned — and that's the most natural setting for secret reprisals, since they can be carried out there with greater safety. There were public and obvious signs that it wouldn't be safe for some of the officers whose duty it was to review them. A council was held, several plans proposed, as in a delicate and high-stakes matter. My own counsel, among the rest, was that they should at all costs avoid giving any sign of suspicion: the officers most at risk should ride boldly through the ranks with bright, confident faces, and instead of skimping on gunfire (as the majority were urging), they should ask the captains to order the soldiers to fire round, full volleys in honour of the spectators, sparing no powder. This was done, and served so well that it pleased the suspect troops and from then on bred mutual confidence and trust among them.

I look on Julius Caesar's way of winning men over as the best and finest you can practise. First he tried by clemency to make himself loved even by his enemies, contenting himself, when conspiracies were detected, with publicly announcing that he was already aware of them. After that, he made the noble resolution to wait without anxiety or fear for whatever might happen, surrendering himself entirely to the protection of the gods and of fortune — for, no question, that's the state he was in when he was killed.

A stranger, having publicly said he could teach Dionysius, the tyrant of Syracuse, an infallible method for uncovering all the conspiracies his subjects could contrive against him, if Dionysius would pay him a good sum for his trouble, was sent for. Dionysius wanted to learn so necessary an art. The man answered that the only art he knew was this: Dionysius should give him a talent of silver and then boast that he'd received an unparalleled secret from him. Dionysius liked the trick, and accordingly had six hundred crowns counted out to him. It wasn't likely he'd give so large a sum to an unknown man except on account of some extraordinary disclosure, and the belief in this kept his enemies on edge. Princes, in fact, are wise to publicise the information they receive about plots against their lives, so as to convince people they have such good intelligence that nothing can be plotted against them without their getting wind of it instantly. The Duke of Athens did many foolish things in setting up his new tyranny over Florence, but one stood out above the rest: receiving the first intimation of a conspiracy the people were hatching against him from Matteo di Morozzo, one of the conspirators, he promptly put Morozzo to death — to suppress the rumour, so that no one would think any of his subjects disliked his government.

I remember reading the story of some Roman of high rank who, fleeing the tyranny of the Triumvirate, had escaped a thousand times, by as many ingenious tricks, from falling into the hands of his pursuers. One day a troop of horse sent out to take him passed close by a thicket where he was crouching and very nearly missed spotting him. He considered, at that moment, the pains and difficulties he'd endured for so long evading the relentless searches made for him every day; the little pleasure he could hope for in such a life; and how much better it would be to die once for all than to live perpetually on this knife-edge. He rose up from his hiding place, called the soldiers back, showed them his form, and voluntarily delivered himself up to their cruelty — by that means freeing both himself and them from further trouble. To invite your enemies in to cut your throat seems an odd, extravagant resolution; and yet I think he did better to take that course than to live in continual feverish fear of an accident there was no cure for. Since all the remedies a man can apply to such a disease are full of restlessness and uncertainty, it's better, with manly courage, to brace oneself for the worst that can happen, and to take some comfort in knowing that the thing we fear may never come to pass.

title: Of pedantry
paragraphs: As a boy I was strangely struck to see in the Italian farces that a pedant was always brought on as the fool of the play, and that the title of Magister enjoyed no greater reverence among us. Since I had been handed over to such men for my education, how could I not be jealous of their honour and reputation? I tried to excuse them by the natural incompatibility between the common sort and men of finer thread, both in judgment and in knowledge — they go quite opposite ways. But what most stuck in my throat was that the finest gentlemen were the ones who most despised them — witness our own famous poet Du Bellay —
"Mais je hay par sur tout un scavoir pedantesque."
["Above all things, I hate pedantic learning." — Du Bellay]

And it was so in earlier times too — for Plutarch says that Greek and Scholar were terms of reproach and contempt among the Romans. Since then, with the better experience of age, I find they had very good reason for it, and that —
"Magis magnos clericos non sunt magis magnos sapientes."
["The greatest scholars are not the wisest men." A proverb given in Rabelais's Gargantua, i. 39.]

But how it comes about that a mind enriched with the knowledge of so many things doesn't become quicker and livelier — that a gross, common understanding can lodge inside it without correcting and improving itself by all the speeches and judgments of the greatest minds the world has ever produced — that I still can't fathom. To take in so many foreign conceptions, fancies so great and so high, a man's own brain (as a young lady, one of the greatest princesses of the kingdom, once said to me of a certain person) must be crowded and squeezed into a smaller compass to make room for the others. I'd be inclined to conclude that, just as plants are smothered by too much nourishment and lamps by too much oil, so the active part of the understanding is by too much study and matter embarrassed and confounded with such a diversity of things that it loses the power to disengage itself, and under the pressure of that weight is bowed, subjected, and doubled up. But the case is quite the opposite: for our soul stretches and dilates as it fills. Among the examples of earlier times we see, on the contrary, men very fit for public business — great captains and great statesmen — who were also very learned.

And as for the philosophers — a sort of men remote from public affairs — they were also sometimes mocked, by the comic licence of their times, for opinions and manners that made them appear ridiculous to men of a different cast. Make them judges of a lawsuit, of human conduct? They're ready to take it on, and immediately begin to ask whether there's life, whether there's motion, whether man is anything other than an ox; what it is to act and to suffer; what kinds of animals law and justice are. Speak about the magistrates, or to one, and they do it with a rude, irreverent, indecent liberty. Let them hear a prince or a king praised, and they think no more of him than of a shepherd, a goatherd, or a herdsman — a lazy Corydon busy milking and shearing his herd, but more roughly and harshly than the herdsman himself. Do you regard a man as great for being lord of two thousand acres? They laugh at such a pitiful little patch, claiming the whole world for their own possession. Do you boast of your nobility, descended from seven rich successive ancestors? They look at you with contempt, as men who have no proper idea of nature's universal picture, and who fail to consider how many ancestors every one of us has had — rich, poor, kings, slaves, Greeks, and barbarians. Even if you were the fiftieth in descent from Hercules, they regard it as great vanity to set such a value on what is merely a gift of fortune. And so the common people scorned them in turn, as men ignorant of the most elementary and ordinary things, presumptuous and insolent.

But this Platonic picture is far different from the way our pedants are presented. The old philosophers were envied for raising themselves above the common sort, for despising the ordinary actions and offices of life, for having taken up a particular and inimitable way of living, and for using a certain elevated and antique mode of speech quite different from ordinary talk. Our pedants, by contrast, are despised for being as far below the usual level as the old philosophers were above it — incapable of public employment, leading a life and adopting the manners of the lowest and basest sort of men:
"Odi ignava opera, philosopha sententia."
["I hate men who chatter about philosophy but do nothing." — Pacuvius, in Gellius, xiii. 8.]

As for the philosophers — as I said — if they were great in knowledge, they were even greater in action. Take the geometer of Syracuse: when he was disturbed at his contemplation to apply his skill to the defence of his country, he immediately set in motion dreadful and prodigious engines that produced effects beyond all human expectation. Yet he himself disdained all his handiwork, thinking that in this he had played the mere mechanic and violated the dignity of his art, of which these performances were only trivial experiments and playthings. So whenever the philosophers have been put to the test of action, they've been seen to rise to such a pitch that it's clear their souls were marvellously elevated and enriched by their knowledge. But some of them, seeing the reins of government in the hands of incompetent men, kept clear of all political administration. Crates, when asked how long it was necessary to philosophise, answered: "Until our armies are no longer commanded by fools." Heraclitus resigned the royalty to his brother; and to the Ephesians, who reproached him for spending his time playing with children before the temple, he said: "Isn't it better to do this than to sit at the helm of affairs in your company?" Others have raised their imagination above the world and fortune, and looked on the tribunals of justice, even the thrones of kings, as paltry and contemptible. Empedocles refused the royalty the Agrigentines offered him. Thales was once arguing against the trouble men take to grow rich, and someone in the company answered that he was like the fox who complained of what he couldn't reach. He had a mind, for the joke's sake, to show the contrary. He gathered up all his wits for the occasion, applied them wholly to profit and gain, set up a trading operation, and in one year brought in such great wealth that the most experienced merchants couldn't, in a whole lifetime of effort, have heaped together so much. As for what Aristotle reports of those who called him, Anaxagoras, and others of their profession wise but not prudent — for not applying their study to more profitable things — I don't really swallow that verbal distinction; nor does it serve to excuse my pedants, for if you look at the low and needy circumstances they're content with, the more reasonable verdict is that they are neither wise nor prudent.

But leaving that first reason aside, I think it better to say this evil comes from their applying themselves to the sciences the wrong way; that, given the manner in which we're taught, it's no wonder neither students nor masters become wiser or more capable, however much more learned. In plain truth, the trouble and expense our parents spend on our education aim at nothing but to furnish our heads with knowledge — not a word of judgment and virtue. Shout out, as someone passes, "There goes a learned man!" — and "There goes a good man!" — and people will turn their eyes and direct their respect to the first. There ought to be a third caller: "There go the blockheads!" Men are quick to ask whether such-and-such a person understands Greek or Latin, whether he's a poet or writes in prose. But whether he's grown better or wiser — qualities of principal concern — never crosses their mind. We should rather ask who is better learned than who is more learned.

We labour only to stuff the memory, leaving the conscience and the understanding empty and bare. Like birds who fly out to forage for grain and bring it home in the beak without tasting it themselves, to feed their young, so our pedants go picking knowledge here and there out of books and hold it at the tip of the tongue — only to spit it out again and pass it on. And here I can't help smiling at how nicely I've paid myself for pointing out this kind of learning's silliness, since I'm so obvious an example of it myself; for don't I do exactly the same thing throughout almost this whole composition? I go here and there, culling out of various books the sentences that best please me, not to keep them (I have no memory to retain them in) but to transplant them into this book; where, to be honest, they are no more mine than they were in their original places. We are, I think, knowing only in present knowledge, not in what's past, any more than in what's to come. But the worst of it is that the scholars and pupils of these pedants are no better nourished by this kind of feeding either; it makes no deeper impression on them, but passes from hand to hand only to make a show, to keep tolerable company, to tell pretty stories — like counterfeit coins in counters, of no other use or value than to reckon with or to bet at cards:
"Apud alios loqui didicerunt non ipsi secum."
["They have learned to speak from others, not from themselves." — Cicero, Tusc. Quaes., v. 36.]
"Non est loquendum, sed gubernandum."
["Speaking is not so important as governing." — Seneca, Ep., 108.]

Nature, to show that there's nothing barbarous where she alone is in charge, often produces, in nations where art has the least to do, works of wit that rival the greatest achievements of art. In relation to what I was just saying, the Gascon proverb derived from a cornpipe is very neat and subtle:
"Bouha prou bouha, mas a remuda lous dits quem."
You may blow till your eyes start out; but if once you try to move your fingers, it's all over.
We can say: Cicero says this; these were Plato's manners; these are the very words of Aristotle. But what do we ourselves say? What do we judge? A parrot could say as much.

And this reminds me of that rich Roman gentleman who'd taken great trouble and expense to find men excellent in every branch of science, kept them always in attendance, so that whenever the conversation among his friends turned to any subject they could supply his place and prompt him — one with a sentence from Seneca, another with a verse from Homer, each according to his speciality. He imagined this knowledge to be his own because it was in the heads of those who lived off his bounty — as do those whose learning consists in owning a fine library. I know one man who, when I ask him what he knows, immediately calls for a book to show me; he wouldn't dare so much as tell me he has piles in his backside until he's first looked up in his dictionary what piles and backsides are.

We take other men's knowledge and opinions on trust — which is an idle, superficial sort of learning. We must make it our own. We're like the man who, needing fire, went to a neighbour's house to fetch some and, finding a very good one there, sat down to warm himself without remembering to carry any back with him. What good does it do us to have a stomach full of meat if it isn't digested, isn't incorporated into us, doesn't nourish and sustain us? Can we imagine that Lucullus, whom letters alone (without any experience) made so great a captain, learned to be so in that perfunctory way? We let ourselves lean so heavily on another man's arm that we destroy our own strength. Do I want to fortify myself against the fear of death? It must be at Seneca's expense. Do I want to extract some consolation for myself or my friend? I borrow it from Cicero. I could have found it in myself if I'd been trained to make use of my own reason. I don't like this dependent, mendicant understanding; for though we can become learned by other men's learning, a man can only be wise by his own wisdom:
["I hate the wise man who is not wise in his own concerns." — Euripides, in Cicero, Ep. Fam., xiii. 15.]
From which Ennius:
"Nequidquam sapere sapientem, qui ipse sibi prodesse non quiret."
["That wise man's wisdom is worth nothing, who can't profit by his own wisdom." — Cicero, De Offic., iii. 15.]
"Si cupidus, si Vanus, et Euganea quantumvis mollior agna."
["If he be grasping, or a boaster, and softer than an Euganean lamb." — Juvenal, Sat., viii. 14.]
"Non enim paranda nobis solum, sed fruenda sapientia est."
["For wisdom is not only to be acquired, but to be put to use." — Cicero, De Finib., i. I.]

Dionysius laughed at the grammarians who set themselves to inquire into the miseries of Ulysses and were ignorant of their own; at musicians so exact in tuning their instruments who never tuned their manners; at orators who made it a study to declare what justice is but never took the trouble to do it. If the mind is no better disposed, if the judgment is no better settled, I'd much rather my pupil had spent his time at tennis — at least his body would be in better shape for it. Watch him when he comes home from school, after fifteen or sixteen years there. There's nothing less fit for employment. All you'll find he's gained is that his Latin and Greek have only made him a bigger coxcomb than he was when he left home. He should bring back a soul filled with good literature, and he brings it back only swelled and puffed up with empty shreds and patches of learning; he really has nothing more in him than he had before.

These pedants of ours, as Plato says of the Sophists their cousins, are of all men the ones who most pretend to be useful to humanity, and yet alone of all men they not only fail to improve what is committed to them — as a carpenter or mason would — but make their charges worse, and make us pay them for making them worse into the bargain. If the rule Protagoras proposed to his pupils were followed — that they should either pay his asking price or swear an oath in the temple as to how much they reckoned the benefit they'd received under his tuition was worth, and pay him accordingly — my pedagogues would find themselves badly stuck if they had to be judged by the affidavits of my experience. My Perigord dialect very neatly calls these pretenders to learning lettre-ferits — letter-stamped, as if letters had been hammered onto them with a mallet. And in truth, for the most part, they appear to be deprived even of common sense. The farmer and the cobbler go simply and honestly about their business, speaking only of what they know and understand; but these fellows, in order to make a show and gain a reputation, parade about their ridiculous knowledge that floats on the surface of the brain, constantly tangling themselves up in their own nonsense. They speak fine words sometimes, true enough — let someone wiser apply them. They're wonderfully well acquainted with Galen, but not at all with the patient's disease; they'll already have deafened you with a long row of laws, while understanding nothing of the case in hand; they have the theory of everything — let who will put it into practice.

I once sat by, at my own house, while a friend of mine, just for sport, counterfeited a jargon of nonsense with one of these fellows — a patchwork of phrases without head or tail, except that he interlarded here and there some terms that had a vague relation to their dispute — and kept the coxcomb in play a whole afternoon, while all the while the man thought he was answering pertinently and learnedly. And yet this was a man of letters, of reputation, a fine gentleman of the long robe:
"Vos, O patricius sanguis, quos vivere par est Occipiti caeco, posticae occurrite sannae."
["O you of patrician blood, to whom it's allowed to live without eyes in the back of your head, beware of the grimaces aimed at you from behind." — Persius, Sat., i. 61.]

Whoever closely examines and thoroughly sifts this sort of people, with whom the world is so pestered, will find, as I have done, that for the most part they understand neither others nor themselves; that their memories are full enough, but their judgment totally empty — with a few exceptions, men whom nature has of itself formed into better shape. I noticed this, for example, in Adrian Turnebus, who, having never professed anything but pure learning, and in that, in my opinion, the greatest man we've seen in a thousand years, had nothing of the pedant in him except the wearing of his gown and a little outward fashion that could never be civilised into courtier ways — which in themselves are nothing. I hate our people who can less easily endure an ill-cut robe than an ill-shaped mind, and who measure a man by the leg he makes, by his behaviour, even by the very fashion of his boots, to judge what kind of man he is. Within Turnebus, there wasn't a more polished soul on earth. I have often deliberately put him onto subjects far from his profession, and found such a clear insight, such a quick apprehension, such a solid judgment, that you'd have thought he'd practised nothing else but arms, and been employed all his life in affairs of state. These are great and vigorous natures,
"Queis arte benigna Et meliore luto finxit praecordia Titan."
["Whom benign Titan (Prometheus) has formed of better clay." — Juvenal, xiv. 34.]
— men who can keep themselves upright despite a pedantic education. But it's not enough that our education does not spoil us; it must, beyond that, alter us for the better.

Some of our Parliaments, when admitting officers, examine only their learning; others also add a test of understanding, by asking their judgment on some legal case. The latter, in my view, proceed by the better method; for although both are necessary, and they should certainly not be deficient in either, knowledge isn't quite so necessary as judgment. Judgment can manage without knowledge, but knowledge can never manage without judgment. As the Greek verse has it —
["To what use is learning, if understanding is absent?" — In Stobaeus, tit. iii., p. 37 (1609).]
Would to God that, for the good of our judicature, these bodies were as well stocked with understanding and conscience as they are with knowledge.
"Non vita, sed scolae discimus."
["We don't study for life, but only for the school." — Seneca, Ep., 106.]

We are not to fasten learning onto the soul, but to work them together, to make them one; not just to tincture it, but to give it a thorough and perfect dye; which, if it won't take colour and improve its imperfect state, it would be much better to leave alone. It's a dangerous weapon, one that will hinder and wound its master, if put into an awkward and unskilled hand:
"Ut fuerit melius non didicisse."
["So that it had been better not to have learned." — Cicero, Tusc. Quaes., ii. 4.]

And this, perhaps, is the reason why neither we nor theology require much learning in women. Francis, Duke of Brittany, son of John V, when someone was talking with him about his marriage to Isabella, daughter of the King of Scotland, and added that she was modestly bred and without any learning, answered that he liked her the better for it, and that a woman was wise enough if she could tell her husband's shirt from his doublet. So it's no great wonder, as some make of it, that our ancestors held letters in no greater esteem, and that even today they're rarely found in the principal councils of princes. If the goal of acquiring wealth, which is the only thing we propose to ourselves through law, medicine, pedantry, and even divinity itself, didn't keep them in credit, you'd see them, no doubt, in as pitiful a condition as ever. And what loss would that be, if they teach us neither to think well nor to do well?
"Postquam docti prodierunt, boni desunt."
[Seneca, Ep., 95. "Since the savants made their appearance among us, the good people have been eclipsed." — Rousseau, Discours sur les Lettres.]
All other knowledge is harmful to one who lacks the knowledge of goodness.

But the reason I just touched on — may it not also come from this, that in France our studies have almost no aim but profit? Apart from those who, by nature born to offices of glory rather than gain, give themselves to letters for so short a time, taken from their studies before they can get any real taste of them, into a profession that has nothing to do with books — those who remain to give themselves wholly to learning are people of low condition, who use it only as a means of livelihood. By such people, whose souls are by nature and by upbringing of the basest alloy, the fruits of knowledge are immaturely gathered, badly digested, and delivered to their recipients as quite a different thing. It is not for knowledge to light up a soul that is dark of itself, nor to make a blind man see. Her business is not to find a man eyes, but to guide, govern, and direct them, provided he has sound feet and straight legs to walk on. Knowledge is an excellent drug, but no drug has the virtue to preserve itself from corruption and decay if the vessel it is kept in is tainted and impure. Such a one may have a sight clear enough, who looks askance, and consequently sees what is good but doesn't follow it; sees knowledge, but doesn't use it. Plato's principal instruction in his Republic is to fit his citizens with employments suited to their nature. Nature can do all, and does all. Cripples are unfit for bodily exercises, and crippled souls are unfit for the exercises of the mind. Degenerate and vulgar souls are unworthy of philosophy. If we see a shoemaker with his shoes out at the toes, we say it's no wonder — for the cobblers commonly go worst shod. In the same way, experience often shows us a doctor in worse health than his patients, a divine less reformed than his flock, and (regularly) a scholar with less wisdom than ordinary people.

Old Aristo of Chios had reason to say that philosophers harmed their listeners — because most of those who heard them weren't capable of deriving any benefit from instruction, which, if not applied to good, would certainly be applied to ill:
["From the school of Aristippus came effeminate debauchees; from that of Zeno, cynics." — Cicero, De Natura Deor., iii., 31.]

In that excellent institution that Xenophon attributes to the Persians, we find they taught their children virtue as other nations taught letters. Plato tells us that the eldest son in their royal succession was brought up like this: after his birth he was delivered, not to women, but to eunuchs of the highest standing about the kings for their virtue, whose charge was to keep his body healthy and in good condition. After he turned seven, they taught him to ride and to hunt. At fourteen he was handed over to four men — the wisest, most just, most temperate, and most valiant of the nation — of whom the first instructed him in religion, the second to be always upright and sincere, the third to master his appetites and desires, and the fourth to despise all danger.

It is a thing worth great consideration, that in the excellent — indeed, for its perfection, prodigious — civil regime laid down by Lycurgus, though so concerned for the education of children as the matter of greatest importance, even at the very seat of the Muses, he makes so little mention of learning, as if that high-spirited youth, disdaining all other subjection but that of virtue, ought to be supplied not with tutors to read them arts and sciences, but with masters who would only instruct them in valour, prudence, and justice — an example Plato followed in his Laws. Their method of discipline was to put questions to the boys about judgments on men and their actions; if the boys praised or condemned this or that person or deed, they had to give a reason for so doing, and by this means they sharpened their understanding and learned what was right. Astyages, in Xenophon, asks Cyrus to give an account of his last lesson, and the lesson went like this: "A big boy in our school, having a short little jacket, took by force a longer one from another boy who wasn't as tall as he was, and gave him his own in exchange. I, being appointed judge of the dispute, ruled that each should keep the coat he had, because each was now better fitted with the other's than with his own. Whereupon my master told me I'd done badly: I had only considered the fit of the garments, when I ought to have considered the justice of the thing, which required that nothing be forcibly taken from anyone that was rightfully his." And Cyrus adds that he was whipped for his pains — just as we are in our villages for forgetting the first aorist of ——.
[Cotton's version of this story begins differently, and includes a passage that doesn't appear in any of the editions of the original I have before me:

"Mandane, in Xenophon, asks Cyrus how he is to learn justice and the other virtues among the Medes, having left all his masters behind in Persia. He answers that he learned those things long ago — that his master had often made him judge of his schoolfellows' disputes, and one day whipped him for giving a wrong sentence." — W.C.H.]

My pedant must give me a very learned oration, in genere demonstrativo, before he'll persuade me that his school is like that one. The Persians knew how to go the most direct way to work; and since the science that's best applied and best understood can do no more than teach us prudence, moral honesty, and resolution, they decided to start by initiating their children into the knowledge of effects — instructing them not by hearsay and rote, but by the experience of action, vividly forming and moulding them, not only by words and precepts but chiefly by deeds and examples, so that it would not just be a knowledge of the mind but its complexion and habit — not an acquisition but a natural possession. Someone once asked Agesilaus what he thought boys should learn most. "What they ought to do when they're men," he said. It's no wonder such an institution produced such admirable effects.

They used to go, it's said, to the other cities of Greece to look for rhetoricians, painters, and musicians; but to Lacedaemon for legislators, magistrates, and generals. At Athens you learned to speak well; here, to do well. There, to disengage yourself from a sophistical argument and untangle the imposture of captious syllogisms; here, to evade the baits and lures of pleasure and, with a noble courage and resolution, to overcome the threats of fortune and death. Those people cudgelled their brains about words; these made it their business to inquire into things. There was an endless babbling of the tongue; here, a continual exercise of the soul. So it's no wonder, when Antipater demanded fifty boys from them as hostages, they answered — quite the opposite of what we would do — that they would rather give him twice as many grown men, so highly did they value the loss of their country's education. When Agesilaus pressed Xenophon to send his sons to Sparta to be brought up, he said: "Not to learn logic or rhetoric, but to be instructed in the noblest of all sciences — the science of obeying and commanding."

It's very pleasing to see Socrates, in his usual manner, rallying Hippias, who recounts to him how much money he's made, especially in certain little villages of Sicily, by teaching school — and that he never made a penny at Sparta. "What a stupid people," said Socrates, "who make no account either of grammar or poetry, and only busy themselves studying the genealogies and successions of their kings, the foundations, rises, and declines of states, and such old wives' tales." After which, having led Hippias step by step to acknowledge the excellence of their public administration and the felicity and virtue of their private life, he leaves him to guess at the conclusion he draws about the uselessness of Hippias's pedantic arts.

Examples have shown us that in military affairs, and all others of that active sort, the study of the sciences softens and saps men's courage rather than strengthening and exciting it. The most powerful empire in the world today is that of the Turks — a people equally trained in the esteem of arms and the contempt of letters. I find Rome was more warlike before she grew so learned. The most warlike nations now in existence are the most rude and ignorant: the Scythians, the Parthians, Tamerlane — proof enough. When the Goths overran Greece, the only thing that preserved the libraries from the fire was that someone convinced them to leave this kind of furniture untouched for the enemy, as the surest way to divert them from arms and fix them in a lazy, sedentary life. When our King Charles VIII found himself master of the kingdom of Naples and a good part of Tuscany almost without striking a blow, the nobles around him put this unexpected ease of conquest down to this: the princes and nobles of Italy were more concerned to make themselves clever and learned than vigorous and warlike.

title: Of the education of children
paragraphs: TO MADAME DIANE DE FOIX, Comtesse de Gurson

I never yet saw a father, however decrepit or deformed his son might be, who didn't still own him. Not that — unless he were totally besotted with paternal affection and blinded by it — he didn't see well enough his son's defects; but with all the defaults, he was still his son. Just so, I see better than anyone that everything I write here is nothing but the idle reveries of a man who has only nibbled at the outer crust of the sciences in his youth and retained only a general, formless image of them; who has a snatch of everything and nothing of the whole, à la française. For I know, in general, that there is such a thing as medicine, such a thing as jurisprudence; four branches in mathematics; and roughly what all of these aim at. And perhaps I know a little further what the sciences in general pretend to do in service of our life. But to dive deeper than that, to have racked my brains over Aristotle, the monarch of all modern learning, or particularly to have devoted myself to any one science — I have never done it. There's not a single art whose first lineaments and rough sketch I could draw. The lowest boy in school could claim to be wiser than I, since I'm not able to examine him in his first lesson; and if I'm ever forced to it, I'm reduced — clumsily enough, in self-defence — to asking him some universal questions to test his natural understanding: a lesson as strange and unfamiliar to him as his is to me.

I never seriously settled down to read any book of solid learning except Plutarch and Seneca; and there, like the Danaids, I'm forever filling and forever leaking; something of it drips onto this paper, but little or nothing stays with me. History is my particular game where reading is concerned, or else poetry, for which I have a particular fondness and esteem. For as Cleanthes said, just as the voice, forced through the narrow throat of a trumpet, comes out sharper and more forceful, so a sentence pressed within the harmony of verse seems to me to dart out more briskly upon the understanding, and strikes my ear and apprehension with a smarter and more pleasing effect. As for the natural parts I have, of which this is the test, I find them bowing under the burden. My fancy and judgment only grope in the dark, tripping and stumbling on the way; and when I've gone as far as I can, I'm in no way satisfied. I still see a new and greater extent of land before me, with a troubled and imperfect sight, wrapped up in clouds I can't penetrate. And as I take it upon myself to write indifferently about whatever comes into my head, using nothing but my own natural means, if I happen to meet, in some good author (as often happens), the same topics I've attempted to write upon — as just now, in Plutarch's "Of the Force of Imagination" — to see myself so weak, so faint, so heavy and flat, in comparison with those better writers, I both pity and despise myself. Yet I take some pleasure in this, that my opinions often have the honour and good fortune to coincide with theirs, that I'm travelling in the same path, though at a very great distance, and can say, "Ah, that is so." I'm further satisfied to find I have one quality that not everyone is blessed with: the ability to see the vast difference between them and me. And in spite of all that, I let my own inventions, low and feeble as they are, run on in their course, without mending or papering over the defects this comparison has laid bare to my view. To be honest, a man needs a strong back to keep pace with such people. The indiscreet scribblers of our times, who among their laborious nothings insert whole sections and pages from ancient authors, hoping by that means to lend lustre to their own writings, do quite the opposite; for the infinite contrast between the ornaments and their own composition makes their own work look so sallow and deformed that they lose much more than they gain.

The philosophers Chrysippus and Epicurus were of two entirely opposite tempers in this: the first not only mixed passages and sayings from other authors into his books, but entire pieces — in one, the whole Medea of Euripides — which gave Apollodorus occasion to say that if a man picked out of his writings everything that was not his, he'd be left with blank paper. Epicurus, on the contrary, in the three hundred volumes he left behind, has not so much as one quotation.

The other day I happened to come across this piece of luck. I was reading a French book where, after long wandering through a great many words so dull, so insipid, so void of wit or common sense that they were really only French words, after a long and tedious slog I came at last to a passage that was lofty, rich, and lifted to the very clouds. Had I found either a gentle slope or a gradual ascent up to it, there'd have been some excuse; but it was so sheer a precipice, so wholly cut off from the rest of the work, that by the first six words I found myself flying off into another world, and from there saw the vale I had climbed out of as so deep and low that I've never had the heart to descend into it again. If I set out one of my discourses with such rich spoils, it would too clearly expose the imperfection of my own writing. To rebuke in others the fault I'm guilty of myself seems to me no more unreasonable than condemning (as I often do) in myself the faults of others; they should be reproved everywhere and given no sanctuary. I know perfectly well how brazenly I try, at every turn, to equal myself to my thefts, to make my style march hand in hand with them, not without an audacious hope of deceiving my reader's eye. But it's as much by the benefit of my application that I hope to do it as by my invention or any force of my own. Besides, I don't pretend to fight the whole body of these champions, nor hand to hand with any single one of them; it's only by skirmishes and light feints that I engage them. I don't grapple with them — I only try their strength, and never push so far as I pretend. If I could hold them in play, I'd be a brave fellow indeed, for I only attack them where they are most sinewy and strong. To cover yourself (as I've seen some do) with another man's armour, so that even your fingertips don't show; to carry on a project (as anyone with a touch of the scholar can do on an ordinary subject) under old inventions patched up here and there with your own scraps, and then to try to conceal the theft and pass it off as your own — that's first an injustice and meanness of spirit in those who do it; since they have nothing of their own fit to win them a reputation, they try to do it by foisting on the world things that aren't theirs at all in their own name. And then it's a ridiculous folly to content yourself with the ignorant approval of the common sort by such a pitiful trick, at the same time degrading yourself in the eyes of men of understanding, who turn up their noses at all that borrowed plaster, even though their praise alone is worth having. For my own part, there's nothing I'd less willingly do; nor have I said so much about others except to get a better chance to explain myself. Nor do I aim, in this, at the composers of centos who openly declare themselves such — of which I've known several very ingenious in my time, particularly one writing under the name of Capilupus, besides the ancients. These are really men of wit, and they make it clear they are, both in that way and in others — as for example Lipsius, in that learned and laborious tissue of his Politics.

Anyway, however inconsiderable these ineptitudes may be, I'll say I never intended to conceal them, any more than the old bald grizzled likeness of myself you'll find at the front, where the painter has given you not a perfect face but mine. For these are my own particular opinions and fancies, offered as what I myself believe, not as what others ought to believe. I have no other end in this writing but to make myself known — myself, who may perhaps be another thing tomorrow, if I happen to meet any new instruction that changes me. I have no authority to be believed, nor do I desire it — being too conscious of my own ignorance to be able to instruct others.
Someone, having seen the preceding chapter, told me the other day at my house that I should have extended my discourse a little further on the education of children.

Now, madam, if I had any competence on this subject, I couldn't employ it better than by offering my best instructions to the little man who threatens you shortly with a happy birth — for you are too generous to begin otherwise than with a male. Having had so great a hand in arranging your marriage, I have a particular interest in the greatness and prosperity of whatever issue comes from it; besides which, your long possession of my service obliges me to wish honour and advantage to everything that concerns you. But in truth, all I understand about this is that the greatest and most important difficulty of human knowledge is the education of children. For as in agriculture the husbandry preceding planting, and the planting itself, is straightforward and well known, but once what is planted comes alive there's a great deal more to be done, more art, more care, more difficulty in cultivating and bringing it to perfection — so it is with men. It's no hard matter to get children; but once they're born, the trouble, anxiety, and care of training, instructing, and bringing them up begins. The signs of their inclinations at that tender age are so obscure, and the promises so uncertain and deceptive, that it's very hard to build any solid judgment or conjecture on them. Look at Cimon, for instance, and Themistocles, and a thousand others, who much disappointed the expectations people had of them. Cubs of bears and puppies readily reveal their natural disposition; but men, as soon as they grow up, settling into certain habits, taking on certain opinions, conforming to particular laws and customs, easily change — or at least disguise — their true and real character. And yet it's hard to force the bent of nature. So, for not having chosen the right course, we often take great pains and waste a good part of our time training up children for things they are by nature totally unfit for. In this difficulty, all the same, I'm clearly of the opinion that they ought to be brought up in the best and most useful studies, without taking too much notice of, or being too superstitious about, the slight prognostics they give of themselves in their tender years — to which Plato, in his Republic, gives, it seems to me, too much weight.

Madam, science is a great ornament and a thing of marvellous use, especially for persons raised to the rank of fortune you are. In truth, in people of mean and low condition it can't perform its true office; for its natural inclination is to assist in the conduct of war, in the government of peoples, in negotiating the leagues and friendships of princes and foreign nations, rather than in framing a syllogism in logic, pleading a case in law, or prescribing a dose of pills in medicine. So, madam, since I'm sure you won't omit so necessary a feature in the education of your children — you yourself having tasted its sweetness, being of a learned line (we still have the writings of the ancient Counts of Foix, from whom your husband and yourself are both descended; and Monsieur de Candale, your uncle, daily obliges the world with more, which will extend the reputation of this quality in your family for many ages to come) — I'll take this occasion to share with you one particular fancy of my own, contrary to the common method, which is all I can contribute to your service in this matter.

The duty of the tutor you'll choose for your son — on whose choice the whole success of his education depends — has several other great responsibilities required by so important a trust besides the one I'm about to speak of; but I won't mention them, since I have nothing of substance to add to the common rules. And in the part where I take it on myself to advise, he may follow me only so far as it seems good advisable.

For a boy of quality, then, who pursues letters not for profit (so mean an object is unworthy of the grace and favour of the Muses, and besides, in it a man directs his service to others, and depends on them), nor so much for outward ornament as for his own proper and peculiar use, to furnish and enrich himself within — wanting rather to come out an accomplished cavalier than a mere scholar or learned man — for such a one, I say, I would have his friends look out for a tutor with a well-made rather than a well-filled head; looking for both, certainly, but rather, between the two, preferring manners and judgment to learning alone; and I'd have this man carry out his task by a new method.

It's the custom of teachers to be eternally booming into their pupil's ears, as if pouring through a funnel, while the pupil's only business is to repeat what they've said. I want a tutor to correct this error, and right from the start, according to the capacity he has to deal with, to put it to the test — letting his pupil taste things himself, and discover and choose for himself, sometimes opening the way for him, sometimes leaving him to open it on his own. That is, I don't want the tutor alone to invent and speak; he should also hear his pupil speak in turn. Socrates, and after him Arcesilaus, first made their pupils speak, and then they spoke to them.
"Obest plerumque iis, qui discere volunt, auctoritas eorum, qui docent."
["The authority of those who teach is often an obstacle to those who want to learn." — Cicero, De Natura Deor., i. 5.]

It's good to make the boy trot ahead like a young horse, so the tutor can judge his pace and how much he has to slow his own to match the other's vigour and capacity. For lack of this proportion we ruin everything; and to know how to adjust it, to keep within a fitting measure, is one of the hardest things I know. It's the effect of a high and well-tempered soul to know how to come down to such childish movements and to govern and direct them. I walk firmer and more securely uphill than down.

Those who, in our common way of teaching, undertake with one and the same lesson and the same dose of direction to instruct several boys of differing and unequal capacities are infinitely mistaken; it's no wonder that out of a whole crowd of pupils, there are scarcely two or three who bring away anything of value from their time. Let the master not only quiz him on the grammatical construction of the bare words of his lesson, but on its sense; and let him judge the boy's progress not by the testimony of his memory but by that of his life. Let the master make him put what he has learned into a hundred different forms, and apply it to as many different subjects, to see whether he properly understands it and has made it his own — drawing his measure of progress from Plato's pedagogic precepts. It's a sign of crudity and indigestion to disgorge our food in the same state we swallowed it; the stomach hasn't done its job unless it has altered the form and condition of what was given it to digest. Our minds work only on trust, when they're bound and compelled to follow another's fancy, enslaved and held captive under the authority of someone else's instruction. We've been so subjected to the harness that we have no free, natural gait of our own; our own vigour and liberty are spent and gone:
"Nunquam tutelae suae fiunt."
["They are ever in tutelage." — Seneca, Ep., 33.]

I was once taken privately at Pisa to see a very honest man, but so great an Aristotelian that his most usual thesis was: "The touchstone and rule of all solid thought, and of all truth, is absolute conformity to Aristotle's doctrine; everything else is nothing but inanity and chimera; for Aristotle has seen everything and said everything." That position, for having been a little too injuriously and broadly interpreted, brought him once into great danger from the Inquisition at Rome, and kept him in it for a long time.

Let the tutor make him examine and thoroughly sift everything he reads, and lodge nothing in his mind on simple authority and trust. Aristotle's principles will then be no more principles to him than those of Epicurus and the Stoics: let this diversity of opinions be laid before him; he will choose, if he is able; if not, he'll remain in doubt.
"Che non men the saver, dubbiar m' aggrata."
["I love to doubt as much as to know." — Dante, Inferno, xi. 93.]

For if he embraces the opinions of Xenophon or Plato by his own reason, they'll no longer be theirs — they'll be his own. He who follows another follows nothing, finds nothing — is, in fact, looking for nothing.
"Non sumus sub rege; sibi quisque se vindicet."
["We are under no king; let each man claim himself for himself." — Seneca, Ep., 33.]

Let him at least know that he knows. He'll need to drink in their knowledge, but not be poisoned by their precepts; and no matter if he forgets where he got his learning, provided he knows how to apply it to his own use. Truth and reason are common to everyone, and belong no more to the one who spoke them first than to the one who speaks them after; it's no more according to Plato than according to me, since both he and I equally see and understand them. Bees cull their various sweets from this flower and that blossom, here and there where they find them, but afterwards they themselves make the honey, which is all and purely their own — no more thyme and marjoram. In the same way, the boy will transform and shuffle together the fragments he borrows from others, to compile a work absolutely his own — that is, his judgment. His instruction, labour, and study aim at nothing else but to form that. He's not obliged to disclose where he got the materials that helped him, but only to show what he himself has done with them. Men who live by pillage and borrowing display their purchases and their buildings to every passer-by; they don't broadcast how they got the money. We don't see a lawyer's fees and perquisites; we see the alliances he uses to fortify himself and his family, and the titles and honours he's secured. No man advertises his income, or at least how it comes in, but everyone publishes his acquisitions. The advantages of our study are to become better and wiser. As Epicharmus says, it's the understanding that sees and hears, the understanding that improves everything, that orders everything, that acts, rules, and reigns; all the other faculties are blind, and deaf, and without soul. And we certainly render it timid and servile by not allowing it the liberty to do anything of itself. Who ever asked his pupil what he thought of grammar and rhetoric, or of such-and-such a sentence of Cicero? Our masters stick them, fully feathered, into our memories, where they're set up like oracles, the letters and syllables themselves treated as the substance of the thing. To know by rote is not to know; it just means to retain what one has entrusted to memory. What a man truly knows and understands he disposes of freely, without reference to the author he got it from or fumbling through the pages of his book. A merely bookish learning is a poor, paltry kind of learning; it may serve for decoration, but it provides no foundation for any structure to be built on it — according to Plato, who says that constancy, faith, and sincerity are the true philosophy, and the other sciences, directed to other ends, are only counterfeit paint. I could wish that Paluel or Pompey, those two famous dancers of my time, could have taught us to cut capers just by watching them, without our stirring from our seats — as these men pretend to inform the understanding without ever setting it to work. Or that we could learn to ride, handle a pike, play the lute, or sing without the trouble of practice, as these try to teach us to judge and speak well without exercising us in judging or speaking. Now in the start of our studies, and in their progress, whatever presents itself to us is book enough: a roguish trick of a page, a stupid mistake of a servant, a joke at the table — all are fresh subjects.

And for this reason, conversation with men is very useful, and so is travel into foreign countries — not to bring back (as most of our young gentlemen do) an account of how many paces around Santa Rotonda is, or the richness of Signora Livia's petticoats, or, as some others, how much Nero's face in some statue in some old ruin is longer or broader than the one on some medal; but mainly to bring back an account of the humours, manners, customs, and laws of the nations where he's been, and so that we may whet and sharpen our wits by rubbing them against those of others. I would have a boy sent abroad very young — and first, to kill two birds with one stone, into those neighbouring nations whose language is most different from our own, and to which, if the tongue isn't shaped early, it grows too stiff to bend.

And it's everyone's opinion, too, that a child shouldn't be brought up in his mother's lap. Mothers are too tender, and their natural affection makes even the most discreet of them so overfond that they can't bring themselves to give the boys the correction they deserve for their faults, nor let them be inured to hardship and risk as they ought to be. They can't bear to see them come back all dust and sweat from their exercises, to drink cold drinks when they're hot, to mount an unruly horse, to take a foil in hand against a rough fencer, or even to fire a carbine. And yet there's no help for it: whoever wants to raise a boy to be good for anything when he grows up must not coddle him while he's young, and must very often break the rules of medicine:
"Vitamque sub dio, et trepidis agat In rebus."
["Let him live in the open air, and always among things that test him." — Horace, Od. ii. 3, 5.]

It's not enough to fortify his soul; you must also make his sinews strong. For the soul will be overburdened if not helped by the body, and would have too hard a task to discharge two offices alone. I know all too well, from my own experience, how mine groans under the burden, weighed down with a body so delicate and indisposed that it leans on her perpetually. And often in my reading I notice that our masters, in their writings, mistake for greatness of soul and fortitude what is really just toughness of skin and hardness of bone. I've seen men, women, and children of such hard and insensible bodily make-up that a sound thrashing meant less to them than a flick on the finger would to me — who wouldn't cry out, wince, or shrink at a serious beating. And when wrestlers impersonate the philosophers in patience, it's rather strength of nerves than stoutness of heart. Now, to be hardened to labour is to be accustomed to enduring pain:
"Labor callum obducit dolori."
["Labour toughens us against pain." — Cicero, Tusc. Quaes., ii. 15.]

A boy must be broken in to the toil and roughness of exercise, so as to be trained up to the pain and suffering of dislocations, colics, cauteries, and even imprisonment and the rack itself — for as the world goes, he may by misfortune come to face the worst of these, which is sometimes inflicted on the good as well as the bad. As proof, in our present civil war, whoever draws his sword against the laws threatens the most honest men with the whip and the halter.

And besides, when he lives at home, the authority of this governor — which ought to be sovereign over the boy entrusted to him — is often checked and hindered by the parents' presence. To which one should also add the respect the whole household pays him as their master's son, and the knowledge he has of the estate and greatness he's heir to: no small drawbacks, in my view, at this tender age.

And even in the conversation with men that I spoke of just now, I've noticed this vice — that instead of gathering observations from others we make it our whole business to lay ourselves open to them, and are more concerned with displaying our own goods than with increasing our stock by acquiring new ones. Silence and modesty are very useful qualities in conversation. The boy should be trained, then, to be sparing and a good steward of his knowledge when he has acquired it; not to take exception to or correct every idle saying or ridiculous story told in his presence; for it's a very unbecoming rudeness to cavil at everything that isn't to our taste. Let him content himself with correcting himself, and not seem to condemn in another anything he wouldn't do himself, nor to dispute against common custom.
"Licet sapere sine pompa, sine invidia."
["One may be wise without ostentation, without envy." — Seneca, Ep., 103.]

Let him avoid the vain and ill-mannered displays of authority, that childish ambition of seeming better bred and better educated than he really is — that bearing will expose itself. And as if opportunities for interrupting and correcting weren't to be passed up, in order to win the reputation of being something more than ordinary. For just as it suits only great poets to make use of poetic licence, so it's intolerable for any but men of great and illustrious souls to claim privileges above the authority of custom:
"Si quid Socrates ant Aristippus contra morem et consuetudinem fecerunt, idem sibi ne arbitretur licere: magnis enim illi et divinis bonis hanc licentiam assequebantur."

["If Socrates or Aristippus did anything contrary to manners and custom, let no one think the same is permitted to him; for it was by great and divine gifts that they obtained this privilege." — Cicero, De Offic., i. 41.]

He should be taught to enter into discourse or dispute only with an opponent worthy of him, and even there not to use every petty trick that might suit his purpose, but only such arguments as best serve him. Let him be taught to be choosy in selecting his reasons, to hate impertinence, and consequently to be brief; but above all, let him be taught to give way and submit to the truth as soon as he discovers it — whether in his opponent's argument or upon better reflection on his own. For he won't be set in the chair just for a clatter of words and syllogisms; he's no further bound to any argument than as he himself approves it; nor is arguing a trade in which the liberty of recanting and changing your mind is to be sold for ready money:
"Neque, ut omnia, qux praescripta et imperata sint, defendat, necessitate ulla cogitur."
["Nor is he under any necessity to defend everything that is prescribed and enjoined him." — Cicero, Acad., ii. 3.]

If his governor is of my temper, he will shape his will to be a very loyal subject to his prince, very affectionate to his person, and very stout in his cause; but at the same time he'll cool in him the desire of having any other tie to that service than public duty. Quite apart from the inconveniences inconsistent with the liberty every honest man ought to have, a man's judgment, when bought and prepossessed by such particular obligations, is either blinded and less free to do its work, or stained with ingratitude and indiscretion. A purely courtier sort of man can neither have the will nor the power to speak or think otherwise than well of a master who has, among so many millions of other subjects, picked him out with his own hand to nourish and advance; this favour, and the profit flowing from it, must necessarily — not without some show of reason — corrupt his frankness and dazzle him. And we commonly see these people speak in a different kind of phrase from what's ordinarily spoken by other people of the same nation, though what they say in that courtly language isn't much to be believed.

Let his conscience and virtue be plainly visible in his speech, with reason alone as their guide. Make him understand that to acknowledge an error in his own argument — even one he himself discovers — is an effect of judgment and sincerity, the principal things he ought to be after; that obstinacy and contention are common qualities, most appearing in mean souls; that to revise and correct himself, to abandon an unjust position in the heat of dispute, are rare, great, and philosophical qualities.

Let him be advised, when in company, to have his eye and ear in every corner; for I find that the seats of greatest honour are usually taken up by men with the least in them, and that the greatest fortunes are rarely accompanied with the ablest parts. I've been present when, while those at the head of the table were only commenting on the beauty of the tapestry or the flavour of the wine, many things very finely said at the lower end were lost and thrown away.
