Let him examine every man's talent — a peasant, a bricklayer, a passer-by — one may learn something from each of these in their own line, and something will be picked out of their talk that may be used at one time or another; even the folly and impertinence of others will contribute to his instruction. By observing the graces and manners of all he sees, he will create in himself an emulation of the good and a contempt of the bad.

Let an honest curiosity be planted in his mind for everything; whatever there is singular or rare near the place where he is, let him go and see it — a fine house, a famous fountain, an eminent man, the field where some ancient battle was fought, the routes of Caesar and Charlemagne:
"Qux tellus sit lenta gelu, quae putris ab aestu, Ventus in Italiam quis bene vela ferat."
["What country is bound by frost, what land is friable with heat, what wind best fills the sails for Italy." — Propertius, iv. 3, 39.]
Let him inquire into the manners, revenues, and alliances of princes — pleasant things in themselves to learn, and very useful to know.

In this conversation with men, I mean also, and chiefly, those who only live in the records of history: by reading those books, he'll converse with the great and heroic souls of the best ages. It's an idle, vain study for those who treat it negligently; but for those who do it with care and observation, it's a study of incalculable value — and the only study, as Plato reports, that the Lacedaemonians reserved for themselves. What profit will he not reap, as to the business of men, by reading Plutarch's Lives! But let my governor remember what end his instructions are mainly directed at, and not so much impress on his pupil's memory the date of Carthage's fall as the manners of Hannibal and Scipio, nor so much where Marcellus died as why it was unworthy of his duty that he died there. Let him not teach him so much the narrative parts of history as how to judge them. The reading of history, in my opinion, is something we apply ourselves to with the most varying degrees of attention. I have read a hundred things in Livy that another has not, or not noticed at least; and Plutarch has read a hundred things there that I never could find, or perhaps that the author never wrote. To some it's merely a grammar exercise; to others the very anatomy of philosophy, by which the most abstruse parts of our human nature are reached. There are in Plutarch many long discourses very worth reading and observing carefully — he is, in my view, of all writers the greatest master in that kind of writing — but there are a thousand others he has only touched and glanced at, where he only points his finger to show us which way we may go if we will, and contents himself with sometimes giving us one brisk hit on the trickiest point of the question, from which we must grope out the rest for ourselves. Take, for example, his saying that the inhabitants of Asia came to be vassals of one man because they couldn't pronounce one syllable, which is "No." That saying perhaps gave La Boétie the matter and occasion to write his "Voluntary Servitude." Just to see him pick out a slight action in a man's life, or a mere word that hardly seems to amount even to that, is itself a whole discourse. It's to our prejudice that men of understanding should so immoderately affect brevity; no doubt their reputation is the better for it, but in the meantime we are the worse for it. Plutarch had rather we should applaud his judgment than commend his knowledge; he had rather leave us with an appetite to read more than glutted with what we've read already. He knew very well that one may say too much even on the best subjects, and that Alexandridas justly reproached someone who made very good but too long speeches to the Ephori, saying: "O stranger! you speak the things you should speak, but not as you should speak them." Those who have lean, spare bodies stuff themselves out with clothes; so those who are short on substance try to make up for it with words.

Human understanding is marvellously enlightened by daily conversation with men, for otherwise we're compressed and heaped up in ourselves, our sight limited to the length of our own noses. Someone asked Socrates what country he was from. He didn't say, of Athens, but of the world. His imagination, fuller and broader, embraced the whole world as his country and extended his society and friendship to all mankind — not like us, who look no further than our feet. When the vines of my village are nipped by frost, my parish priest immediately concludes that God's wrath has gone out against the whole human race, and that the cannibals already have the pip. Who, seeing the havoc of our civil wars, doesn't cry out that the machine of the world is near dissolution, that the Day of Judgment is upon us — without considering that many worse things have happened before, and that meanwhile people are quite merry in a thousand other parts of the earth despite all this? For my part, considering the license and impunity that always attend such commotions, I'm amazed they're so moderate, and that there's no more harm done. To him who feels the hailstones patter about his ears, the whole hemisphere appears to be in storm and tempest — like the ridiculous Savoyard who said very gravely that if that simple king of France could have managed his fortune as he should, he might in time have come to be steward of the household to the duke his master: the fellow couldn't, in his shallow imagination, conceive that there could be anything greater than a Duke of Savoy. And in truth we are all, without realising it, in this same error — an error of great weight and very pernicious consequence. But whoever shall picture to himself, as in a painting, that great image of our mother nature in her full majesty and lustre — whoever shall read in her face so general and so constant a variety, and shall observe himself in that picture, and not himself but a whole kingdom, as no more than the least touch or prick of a pencil compared to the whole — that man alone is able to value things according to their true measure and grandeur.

This great world, which some still multiply as several species under one genus, is the mirror in which we are to see ourselves, in order to know ourselves rightly. In short, I would have this be the book my young gentleman studies most attentively. So many humours, so many sects, so many judgments, opinions, laws, and customs teach us to judge rightly of our own, and inform our understanding to discover its imperfections and natural infirmity — no trivial speculation. So many revolutions of states and kingdoms, so many turns of public fortune, will make us wise enough to make no great wonder of our own. So many great names, so many famous victories and conquests drowned and swallowed in oblivion render ridiculous our hopes of immortalising our names by capturing half a dozen light horse or a chicken coop, which derives its memory only from its ruin. The pride and arrogance of so many foreign pomps, the inflated majesty of so many courts and grandeurs, accustom and harden our sight without dazzling our eyes — so we can endure the lustre of our own. So many trillions of men buried before us encourage us not to fear going to seek such good company in the other world. And so on with the rest. Pythagoras used to say that our life resembles the great and crowded assembly of the Olympic games, where some exercise their bodies to carry off the glory of the prize, others bring merchandise to sell for profit; there are also some (and not the worst sort) who seek no other advantage than to look on and consider how and why everything is done, to be spectators of the lives of other men, so as to judge of and regulate their own better.
To examples may aptly be applied all the profitable discourses of philosophy, by which, as by their best rule, all human actions ought to be directed. A pupil shall be taught to know —

"Quid fas optare: quid asper Utile nummus habet: patrix carisque propinquis Quantum elargiri deceat: quern te Deus esse Jussit, et humana qua parte locatus es in re; Quid sumus, et quidnam victuri gignimur."

["Learn what it's right to wish for; what the proper use of money is; how much we ought to give in liberality to our country and our dear relations; whom and what God commanded you to be; in what part of the human scheme you've been placed; what we are, and to what purpose we are born." — Persius, iii. 69.]

— what it is to know, and what to be ignorant; what the end and design of study ought to be; what valour, temperance, and justice are; the difference between ambition and avarice, between servitude and subjection, between licence and liberty; by what token one may know true and solid contentment; how far death, affliction, and disgrace are to be feared;
"Et quo quemque modo fugiatque feratque laborem."
["And how to shun or bear every hardship." — Virgil, Aeneid, iii. 459.]

— by what secret springs we move, and the reason for our various agitations and irresolutions. For, in my view, the first doctrine with which a man's understanding should be seasoned ought to be the one that regulates his manners and his judgment, that teaches him to know himself, and how both to die well and to live well. Among the liberal sciences, let's begin with the one that makes us free: not that they don't all serve, in some measure, the instruction and use of life, as all other things in some way do too, but let's choose the one that directly and professedly serves that end. If once we can confine the offices of human life within their just and natural limits, we'll find that most of the sciences in use are of no great use to us, and that even in those that are, there are many quite unnecessary cavities and dilations which we'd be better off leaving alone, and, following Socrates' direction, limit the course of our studies to those things where there's a true and real utility:
"Sapere aude; Incipe; Qui recte vivendi prorogat horam, Rusticus exspectat, dum defluat amnis; at ille Labitur, et labetur in omne volubilis oevum."

["Dare to be wise; begin! He who puts off the hour of living well is like the clown waiting for the river to flow out: but the river still flows, and will keep flowing, in unceasing course, through all ages." — Horace, Ep., i. 2.]
It's great foolery to teach our children:
"Quid moveant Pisces, animosaque signa Leonis, Lotus et Hesperia quid Capricornus aqua,"
["What influence Pisces have, or the sign of raging Leo, or Capricorn, bathed by the Hesperian wave." — Propertius, iv. I, 89.]
— the knowledge of the stars and the motion of the eighth sphere before their own:
["What do I care about the Pleiades, or the stars of Taurus?" — Anacreon, Ode, xvii. 10.]

Anaximenes, writing to Pythagoras, said: "To what purpose should I trouble myself searching out the secrets of the stars, when I have death or slavery continually before my eyes?" — for the kings of Persia were at that moment preparing to invade his country. Every man ought to say the same: "Being assaulted as I am by ambition, avarice, rashness, superstition, having so many other enemies of life within, am I to go pondering the world's changes?"

After teaching him what will make him more wise and good, you may then engage him with the elements of logic, physics, geometry, rhetoric — and whichever science he then inclines to most, his judgment being already formed and fit to choose, he'll quickly make his own. The way of teaching him ought to be sometimes by conversation, sometimes by reading; sometimes his tutor will put into his hands the very author he thinks most suitable, sometimes only the marrow and substance of him. And if the tutor himself isn't familiar enough with the books to turn to all the fine passages they contain for his purpose, there may be some scholar joined to him who, whenever the occasion arises, will supply him with what he needs to pass on to his pupil. And who can doubt but this way of teaching is much easier and more natural than that of Gaza, in which the precepts are so intricate and so harsh, and the words so empty, lean, and meaningless, that there's no purchase on them — nothing that quickens and elevates the mind and imagination — whereas here the mind has something to feed on and digest. The fruit of this method is not only without comparison much fairer and more beautiful, but will also ripen much earlier.

It's a thousand pities that matters should be at such a pass in this age of ours, that philosophy, even with men of understanding, is looked on as a vain and fantastic name, a thing of no use or value, either in opinion or in effect — of which I think those quibbles and petty sophistries that block the entrance to it are the cause. People are much to blame for representing philosophy to children as a thing of such difficult access, with such a frowning, grim, and formidable aspect. Who has disguised her like this, with that false, pale, ghostly countenance? There's nothing more airy, more cheerful, more frolicsome — I had almost said, more wanton. She preaches nothing but feasting and merriment; a melancholy, anxious look shows she doesn't live there. Demetrius the grammarian, finding a knot of philosophers sitting and chatting together in the temple at Delphi, said to them: "Either I'm much mistaken, or, by your cheerful and pleasant faces, you're not engaged in any very deep discussion." To which one of them, Heracleon the Megarean, replied: "It's for those who are puzzling whether the future tense of such-and-such a verb is spelt with a double A, or hunting after the derivation of the comparatives and superlatives, to knit their brows while talking of their science; but philosophical discourse always cheers and gladdens those who pursue it, and never makes them sad or downcast."
"Deprendas animi tormenta latentis in aegro Corpore; deprendas et gaudia; sumit utrumque Inde habitum facies."
["You may discern the torments of mind lurking in a sick body; you may also discern its joys; the face takes its character from either of them." — Juvenal, ix. 18.]

The soul that lodges philosophy ought to be of such a constitution of health as to render the body in like manner healthy. Her tranquillity and satisfaction ought to shine outwardly, and her contentment to shape the outward bearing to her own mould, and consequently to fortify it with a graceful confidence, an active and joyous carriage, and a serene and contented look. The most manifest sign of wisdom is a continual cheerfulness; her state is like that of things in the regions above the moon, always clear and serene. It's Baroco and Baralipton that render their disciples so grimy and dispiriting, not she — they don't even know her except by hearsay. What! She is the one who calms and appeases the storms and tempests of the soul, who teaches famine and fevers to laugh and sing — and not by certain imaginary epicycles, but by natural and manifest reasons. She has virtue for her end, which is not, as the schoolmen say, located at the top of a sheer, rugged, inaccessible precipice. Those who have come near her have found her, on the contrary, seated in a fair, fruitful, flowering plain, from which she easily sees everything beneath her — and to which place anyone may come, if he knows the way, through shady, green, sweetly flowering avenues, by an easy and gentle descent, like that of the vault of heaven. It's because some haven't frequented this supreme, beautiful, triumphant, lovable virtue — equally delightful and brave, an avowed enemy to anxiety, sorrow, fear, and constraint, with nature for her guide and fortune and pleasure for her companions — that they've gone, according to their own weak imagination, and made up that ridiculous, sorrowful, querulous, spiteful, threatening, terrible image of her, and set it on a rock among thorns and brambles, and made of her a bogeyman to frighten people with.

But the governor I would have — one who knows it's his duty to fill his pupil with as much or more affection for virtue as reverence for it — will be able to inform him that the poets have always followed the public mood, and to make him understand that the gods have planted more toil and sweat in the avenues to Venus's chambers than in those of Minerva. And when he sees the boy beginning to take notice, and presents him with a Bradamante or an Angelica for a mistress — a natural, active, generous, not mannish but manly beauty, in comparison with a soft, delicate, artificial, simpering, affected one; the one in the dress of a heroic youth, wearing a glittering helmet, the other tricked up in curls and ribbons like a wanton minx — he'll then regard his own affection as brave and manly, when he picks the opposite of that effeminate shepherd of Phrygia.

Such a tutor will make a pupil digest this new lesson, that the height and value of true virtue lies in the ease, utility, and pleasure of its exercise; so far from difficulty that boys as well as men, the innocent as well as the cunning, can make it their own — it is by order, not by force, that it's to be acquired. Socrates, her first favourite, is so averse to all kinds of violence as to throw it aside entirely, and slip into the more natural ease of her own progress. She is the nursing mother of all human pleasures; by making them just, she also makes them pure and lasting; by moderating them, she keeps them sharp and inviting; by forbidding the ones she herself refuses, she whets our appetite for the ones she allows; and like a kind and generous mother she abundantly allows whatever nature requires, even to satiety, if not to weariness — unless we mean to say that the regimen that stops the toper before he's drunk himself blind, the glutton before he's eaten himself sick, and the lecher before he catches the pox is an enemy to pleasure. If the ordinary good fortune fails her, she does without it, and forms another that is wholly her own, less fickle and unsteady than the other. She can be rich, be powerful and wise, and knows how to lie on soft perfumed beds; she loves life, beauty, glory, and health; but her proper and peculiar office is to know how to regulate the use of all these good things, and how to lose them without distress — an office much more noble than troublesome, and without which the whole course of life is unnatural, turbulent, and deformed. And it is there indeed that men may justly picture those monsters on rocks and precipices.

If this pupil should happen to be of so contrary a disposition that he'd rather hear a tall tale than the true account of some noble expedition or some wise and learned discourse; who, at the beat of the drum that fires up the youthful ardour of his companions, leaves it to follow another that calls him to a morris dance or the bear-baiting; who wouldn't sooner choose, and find it more delightful and more excellent, to come home all dust and sweat in victory from a battle than from tennis or a ball with the prize of those exercises — I see no remedy but for him to be apprenticed in some good town to learn to make mince pies, even if he were a duke's son; according to Plato's precept, that children are to be placed and disposed of, not according to the wealth, qualities, or condition of their father, but according to the faculties and capacities of their own souls.
Since philosophy is what teaches us to live, and since childhood has its lessons there as well as other ages, why is it not communicated to children early?
"Udum et molle lutum est; nunc, nunc properandus, et acri Fingendus sine fine rota."
["The clay is moist and soft: now, now make haste, and shape the pitcher on the swift wheel." — Persius, iii. 23.]

They begin to teach us to live when we have almost done living. A hundred students have caught the pox before coming to read Aristotle's lecture on temperance. Cicero said that even if he lived for two men's lifetimes, he would never find leisure to study the lyric poets — and I find these sophists yet more deplorably useless. The boy we're going to bring up has even less time to spare: he owes only the first fifteen or sixteen years of his life to education; the rest is due to action. So let's spend that short time on necessary instruction. Away with the thorny subtleties of dialectic — they're abuses, things by which our lives can never be improved. Take the plain philosophical discourses, learn how to choose them rightly and then to apply them rightly; they're easier to understand than one of Boccaccio's novellas; a child fresh from the nurse is much more capable of them than of learning to read or write. Philosophy has discourses proper for childhood, as well as for the decrepit age of men.

I'm of Plutarch's mind that Aristotle did not so much trouble his great pupil with the knack of framing syllogisms, or with the elements of geometry, as with instilling good precepts about valour, prowess, magnanimity, temperance, and the contempt of fear — and with this ammunition, sent him out, while still a boy, with no more than thirty thousand foot, four thousand horse, and only forty-two thousand crowns, to subdue the empire of the whole earth. For the other arts and sciences, Plutarch says, Alexander highly praised their excellence and charm, and held them in great honour and esteem, but was not so ravished by them as to be tempted to practise them himself:
"Petite hinc, juvenesque senesque, Finem ammo certum, miserisque viatica canis."
["Young men and old, get from here a certain end for the mind, and provisions for wretched grey hairs." — Persius, v. 64.]

Epicurus, at the beginning of his letter to Menoeceus, says, "Neither should the youngest refuse to philosophise, nor the oldest grow weary of it." To do otherwise is to imply that either the time for living happily isn't yet come, or that it's already past. And yet, for all that, I wouldn't want this pupil of ours imprisoned and made a slave to his book; nor would I have him given up to the moroseness and melancholy of a sour, ill-natured pedant.

I wouldn't have his spirit broken and crushed by putting him to the rack and tormenting him, as some do, for fourteen or fifteen hours a day, making a packhorse of him. Nor would I think it good, when by reason of a solitary and melancholy temperament he's discovered to be overly addicted to his book, to feed that humour in him; for that renders him unfit for civil conversation, and diverts him from better employments. How many have I seen in my time totally brutified by an immoderate thirst for knowledge? Carneades was so besotted with it that he wouldn't take time even to comb his hair or pare his nails. Nor would I have his generous manners spoiled by the rudeness and barbarism of someone else's. The French wisdom was anciently proverbial: "Early ripe, soon over." And in truth we still see that nothing can be more clever and pleasing than the children of France; but they usually disappoint the hopes and expectations conceived of them, and grown men, they have nothing extraordinary worth noticing. I've heard men of good understanding say that these colleges of ours, to which we send our young people (and we have far too many), make them into such animals as they are.

But for our little gentleman, a closet, a garden, the table, his bed, solitude, company, morning and evening, all hours shall be the same, and every place a place of study. For philosophy, who as the shaper of judgment and manners shall be his principal lesson, has the privilege of being a part of everything. The orator Isocrates, being asked at a feast to speak of his art, made an answer that satisfied and won the praise of all the company: "It's not now the time," he said, "to do what I can do; and what is now to be done, I can't do." To make orations and rhetorical debates in a company gathered to laugh and feast would have been quite improper, and as much could be said of all the other sciences. But as for philosophy, that part of it at least that treats of man and his offices and duties, it has been the common opinion of all wise men that, out of respect for the sweetness of her conversation, she should be admitted to all sports and entertainments. And Plato, having invited her to his banquet, we see in what gentle and obliging a manner — accommodated to time and place — she entertained the company, even on a discourse of the highest and most important nature:
"Aeque pauperibus prodest, locupletibus aeque; Et, neglecta, aeque pueris senibusque nocebit."
["It profits poor and rich alike; and, neglected, equally hurts young and old." — Horace, Ep., i. 25.]

By this method of instruction, my young pupil will be much better and more usefully employed than his fellows in the college. But just as the steps we take in walking up and down a gallery, though three times as many, don't tire a man so much as those taken on a formal journey, so our lesson, occurring as if by accident, without any set obligation of time or place, and falling naturally into every action, will insinuate itself imperceptibly. Even our exercises and recreations — running, wrestling, music, dancing, hunting, riding, and fencing — will be a good part of our study. I would have his outward fashion and bearing, and the disposition of his limbs, shaped at the same time as his mind. It's not a soul, it's not a body that we're training up, but a man — and we ought not to split him in two. As Plato says, we shouldn't fashion one without the other, but make them draw together like two horses harnessed to a coach. By that saying, doesn't he seem to allow more time and care for the body's exercises, and to hold that the mind, in good proportion, does her work at the same time too?

For the rest, this method of education should be carried on with a stern sweetness, quite contrary to the practice of our pedants, who, instead of tempting and luring children into letters by apt and gentle means, present nothing in fact but rods and ferules, horror and cruelty. Away with this violence! Away with this compulsion! Nothing, I'm convinced, more dulls and degenerates a well-born nature. If you would have him fear shame and chastisement, don't harden him to them. Inure him to heat and cold, to wind and sun, and to dangers he ought to despise; wean him from all effeminacy and delicacy in clothes and lodging, eating and drinking; accustom him to everything, so he may not be a Sir Paris, a carpet-knight, but a sinewy, hardy, vigorous young man. From childhood to my present age I've been of this opinion, and I'm still of it. But among other things, the strict regime of most of our colleges has always displeased me; they could perhaps have erred less harmfully on the indulgent side. It's a real house of correction for imprisoned youth. They're made debauched by being punished before they've done anything to deserve it. Just walk in when they're at their lessons and you'll hear nothing but the cries of boys being beaten and the thunder of pedagogues drunk with fury. A pretty way that, to lure these tender and timorous souls to love their books — with a furious face and a rod in hand! A cursed and pernicious method! Besides what Quintilian has very well observed, that this imperious authority is often followed by very dangerous consequences, and particularly our way of chastising. How much more decent would it be to see their classrooms strewn with green leaves and fine flowers than with the bloody stumps of birch and willow! If it were left to me, I'd paint the school with pictures of joy and gladness, Flora and the Graces, as the philosopher Speusippus did his. Where their profit is, let them also have their pleasure. The food that's proper and wholesome for children should be sweetened with sugar, and what's dangerous to them embittered with gall. It's marvellous to see how careful Plato is in his Laws about the gaiety and diversions of the youth of his city, and how much and how often he expatiates on the races, sports, songs, leaps, and dances — of which, he says, antiquity gave the ordering and patronage specifically to the gods themselves, to Apollo, Minerva, and the Muses. He goes on at length and is very particular in giving countless precepts for exercises; but as for the lettered sciences, he says very little, and only seems to recommend poetry on account of music.

All singularity in our manners and conditions is to be avoided, as inconsistent with civil society. Who wouldn't be astonished at so strange a constitution as that of Demophoön, steward to Alexander the Great, who sweated in the shade and shivered in the sun? I've seen people who fled the smell of a ripe apple more swiftly than from the shot of a harquebus; others afraid of a mouse; others who threw up at the sight of cream; others ready to faint at the making of a feather bed; Germanicus could endure neither the sight nor the crowing of a cock. I won't deny there may, perhaps, be some hidden cause and natural aversion in these cases; but in my opinion a man could overcome it, if he took it in time. Precept has worked so effectively on me, though not without some effort, I confess, that, beer excepted, my appetite accommodates itself indifferently to all sorts of food. Young bodies are supple; one should therefore at that age bend and shape them to all fashions and customs. And provided one can keep the appetite and the will within their due limits, let a young man, in God's name, be made fit for all nations and all companies, even for debauchery and excess if need be — that is, where he does it in compliance with the customs of the place. Let him be able to do anything, but love to do nothing but what is good. The philosophers themselves don't justify Callisthenes for forfeiting his master Alexander's favour by refusing to pledge him a cup of wine. Let him laugh, play, drink, even wench with his prince. Indeed I'd have him, even in his debauches, outdo the rest of the company, and excel his companions in ability and stamina — and that he may not stop doing it for want of power or knowledge how, but only for want of will.
"Multum interest, utrum peccare ali quis nolit, an nesciat."
["There's a vast difference between refusing to sin and not knowing how." — Seneca, Ep., 90.]

I once thought I was paying a compliment to a lord, as free of those excesses as any man in France, by asking him in front of a great deal of very good company how many times in his life he'd been drunk in Germany, while on the king's business there. He took it as I meant it, and answered, "Three times" — and told us the whole story of his debauches. I know some men who, for want of this faculty, have run into great trouble negotiating with that nation. I've often reflected with great admiration on the wonderful constitution of Alcibiades, who could so easily transform himself into so many different fashions without any harm to his health — one while outdoing the Persian pomp and luxury, another the Spartan austerity and frugality; as reformed in Sparta as he was voluptuous in Ionia:
"Omnis Aristippum decuit color, et status, et res."
["Every colour of life, every situation and circumstance, suited Aristippus." — Horace, Ep., xvii. 23.]
I would have my pupil to be such a one —
"Quem duplici panno patentia velat, Mirabor, vitae via si conversa decebit, Personamque feret non inconcinnus utramque."
["I should admire him who, patiently wearing a patched garment, also bears well a changed fortune, playing both parts equally well." — Horace, Ep., xvii. 25.]

These are my lessons. He who puts them into practice will reap more advantage than he who only has had them read to him, and so only knows them. If you see him, you hear him; if you hear him, you see him. God forbid, says someone in Plato, that to philosophise should be only to read a great many books and to learn the arts.
"Hanc amplissimam omnium artium bene vivendi disciplinam, vita magis quam literis, persequuti sunt."
["They have pursued this greatest of all arts — the discipline of living well — by their lives rather than by their reading." — Cicero, Tusc. Quaes., iv. 3.]

Leo, prince of the Phliasians, asked Heraclides Ponticus what art or science he professed. "I know," he said, "neither art nor science, but I am a philosopher." When someone reproached Diogenes that, being ignorant, he should pretend to philosophy, he answered, "For that very reason, I pretend to it the more." Hegesias begged him to read him a certain book. "You're amusing," he said. "You pick figs that are true and natural, not those that are painted; why don't you also choose exercises that are naturally true, rather than those in writing?"

The boy won't so much get his lesson by heart as practise it. He'll repeat it in his actions. We shall discover whether there's prudence in his exercises, whether there's sincerity and justice in his conduct, whether there's grace and judgment in his speech; whether there's constancy in his sickness, modesty in his mirth, temperance in his pleasures, order in his domestic economy, indifference in his palate — whether what he eats or drinks be flesh or fish, wine or water:
"Qui disciplinam suam non ostentationem scientiae, sed legem vitae putet: quique obtemperet ipse sibi, et decretis pareat."
["Who treats his own discipline not as a vain showing-off of science, but as a law and rule of life; and who obeys himself, and the decrees he has set himself." — Cicero, Tusc. Quaes., ii. 4.]

The conduct of our lives is the true mirror of our doctrine. Zeuxidamus, asked why the Lacedaemonians didn't commit their rules of chivalry to writing and hand them to their young men to read, answered that it was because they wanted to inure them to action, not amuse them with words. Compare such a one, after fifteen or sixteen years of study, with one of our college Latinists who has thrown away that much time on nothing but learning to speak. The world is nothing but chatter; I have hardly ever yet seen a man who didn't rather prate too much than say too little. And yet half our lives are wasted that way: we're kept four or five years just to learn words and tack them together into clauses; as many more to form them into a long discourse divided into four or five parts; and another five at least to learn to mix and interweave them subtly and intricately. Let us leave all this to those who make a profession of it.

Going one day to Orleans, I met on the plain this side of Clery two pedants travelling toward Bordeaux, about fifty paces apart; and a good way behind them, I noticed a troop of horse, with a gentleman at their head who was the late Monsieur le Comte de la Rochefoucauld. One of my men asked the leading master of arts who that gentleman was that came after him. He, not having seen the train that followed, and thinking his companion was meant, answered pleasantly, "He's not a gentleman; he's a grammarian; and I am a logician." Now we, who, on the contrary, do not pretend to be breeding a grammarian or a logician but a gentleman, let us leave them to abuse their leisure; our business lies elsewhere. Let our pupil only be well furnished with things, and words will follow fast enough; he'll pull them after him if they don't come voluntarily. I've heard people make excuses that they can't express themselves, pretending to have their minds full of a great many fine things which, for lack of eloquence, they can't bring out. It's a mere pretext, nothing else. Do you want to know what I think of it? I think they're nothing but shadows of some imperfect images and conceptions they don't know what to make of, and consequently can't bring out. They don't yet understand themselves what they're trying to say, and if you just watch how they haggle and stammer on the verge of delivery, you'll soon conclude that their labour is not in giving birth but in conception — that they're still licking their formless embryo. For my part I hold, and Socrates lays it down, that whoever has a sprightly and clear conception in his mind will express it well enough in one language or another, and, if he's mute, by signs.
"Verbaque praevisam rem non invita sequentur;"
["Once a thing is conceived in the mind, the words to express it readily follow." ("The words will not reluctantly follow the thing already conceived.") — Horace, De Arte Poetica, v. 311.]
And as another, as poetically, says in his prose:
"Quum res animum occupavere, verbs ambiunt,"
["When things have taken possession of the mind, words come crowding in." — Seneca, Controvers., iii. proem.]
And another:
"Ipsae res verbs rapiunt."
["The things themselves carry off the words to express them." — Cicero, De Finib., iii. 5.]

He knows nothing of ablative, conjunctive, substantive, or grammar — no more than his footman, or a fishwife on the Petit Pont — and yet they'll give you a bellyful of talk if you'll listen, and perhaps stumble as little in their language as the best masters of art in France. He knows no rhetoric, no way of buttering up the gentle reader with a preface; and he doesn't care to know it. All this fine paint is easily rubbed off by the lustre of a simple and blunt truth; these flourishes only serve to amuse the common sort, who can't take in more solid and nourishing diet, as Aper very evidently shows in Tacitus. The ambassadors of Samos, having prepared a long and elegant oration, came to Cleomenes, king of Sparta, to incite him to war against the tyrant Polycrates. After listening to their speech with great gravity and patience, he gave them this answer: "As for the exordium, I don't remember it, nor consequently the middle of your speech; and as to the conclusion, I won't do what you ask." A very neat answer, I think, and a pack of learned orators very sweetly stuck. And what about the other man? The Athenians were to choose one of two architects for a very great building they had designed. The first, a pert affected fellow, offered his services in a long premeditated discourse on the subject of the work, and by his eloquence won the votes of the people. But the other said only three words: "Athenians, what this man says, I will do." When Cicero was in the heat and flow of an eloquent harangue, many were struck with admiration; but Cato only laughed, saying, "We have a comical consul." Let it come before or after, a good sentence, or something well said, is always in season; if it doesn't fit well with what went before, nor cohere much with what follows, it's good in itself. I'm not one of those who think that good rhyme makes a good poem. Let a man make short long and long short if he likes — it's no great matter; if there's invention, and if the wit and judgment have done their work, I'll say, "There's a good poet, but a poor rhymer."
"Emunctae naris, durus componere versus."
["Of delicate sense, but of rugged versification." — Horace, Sat., iv. 8.]
Let a man, says Horace, strip his work of all method and measure —
"Tempora certa modosque, et, quod prius ordine verbum est, Posterius facias, praeponens ultima primis Invenias etiam disjecti membra poetae."

["Take away the fixed rhythms and measures, and make the word that was first in order come later, putting last things first — you'll still find the limbs of the scattered poet." — Horace, Sat., i. 4, 58.]

— he'll be none the more lost for it; the very pieces will still be fine in themselves. Menander's answer had this meaning: reproved by a friend, the deadline for a comedy he'd promised drawing near, that he hadn't yet started on it, he said, "It's made, and ready — all but the verses." Having framed the subject and arranged the scenes in his head, he set little store by the rest. Since Ronsard and Du Bellay gave our French poetry its reputation, every little dabbler, as far as I see, puffs up his words as high and makes his cadences nearly as harmonious as theirs:
"Plus sonat, quam valet."
["More sound than sense." — Seneca, Ep., 40.]

There were never so many poetasters among the common sort as now; but though they find it no hard task to imitate their rhymes, they fall infinitely short of imitating the rich descriptions of the one and the delicate invention of the other of those masters.

But what will become of our young gentleman if he's attacked by the sophistic subtlety of some syllogism — "A Westphalia ham makes a man drink; drink quenches thirst: therefore a Westphalia ham quenches thirst"? Why, let him laugh at it; it'll be more discreet to do so than to set out to answer it. Or let him borrow this pleasant evasion from Aristippus: "Why should I trouble myself to untie what gives me so much trouble even bound?" When someone tried this dialectical juggling against Cleanthes, Chrysippus cut him short, saying, "Reserve these baubles to play with children, and don't divert the serious thoughts of a grown man with such fooleries." If these ridiculous subtleties —
"Contorta et aculeata sophismata,"

— as Cicero calls them, are designed to make him believe an untruth, they are dangerous; but if they only mean to make him laugh, I don't see why a man needs to be fortified against them. Some go a mile out of their way to hook in a fine word:
"Aut qui non verba rebus aptant, sed res extrinsecus arcessunt, quibus verba conveniant."
["Who don't fit words to the subject, but go searching outside for things that will fit the words." — Quintilian, viii. 3.]
And as another says,
"Qui, alicujus verbi decore placentis, vocentur ad id, quod non proposuerant scribere."
["Who, by their fondness for some fine-sounding word, are tempted into something they had no intention of treating." — Seneca, Ep., 59.]

For my part, I'd rather drag in a fine sentence by head and shoulders to fit my purpose than divert my purpose to hunt after a sentence. On the contrary, words are to serve, and to follow a man's purpose; and let Gascon come into play where French won't do. I would have things so excelling, and so wholly filling the imagination of the listener, that he should have something else to do besides thinking about words. The way of speaking I love is natural and plain, the same in writing as in speaking — a sinewy and muscular way of expressing oneself, short and pithy, not so elegant and artificial as prompt and vehement;
"Haec demum sapiet dictio, qux feriet;"
["That speech indeed will have a savour which strikes the ear." — Epitaph on Lucan, in Fabricius, Biblioth. Lat., ii. 10.]

— rather hard than wearisome; free from affectation; irregular, broken, and bold; where every piece makes up an entire body; not like a pedant, a preacher, or a pleader, but rather a soldierly style, as Suetonius calls that of Julius Caesar — though I see no reason why he should call it that. I've always been inclined to imitate the careless dress that's still observable among the young men of our time — to wear my cloak on one shoulder, my cap on one side, a stocking in disorder — as if to express a kind of haughty disdain for these outlandish ornaments and a contempt for the artificial. But I find this negligence of much better use in the form of speaking. All affectation, particularly in the French gaiety and freedom, is ungraceful in a courtier; and in a monarchy every gentleman ought to be fashioned according to the court model. So an easy, natural negligence does well. I no more like a web where the knots and seams show, than a fine figure so delicate that you can count all the bones and veins:
"Quae veritati operam dat oratio, incomposita sit et simplex."
["Let the language that is dedicated to truth be plain and unaffected." — Seneca, Ep., 40.]
"Quis accurat loquitur, nisi qui vult putide loqui?"
["Who speaks meticulously, except one who wants to speak affectedly?" — Idem, Ep., 75.]

That eloquence prejudices the subject it would advance, which wholly draws us to itself. And as it's a ridiculous effeminacy in our outward dress to distinguish ourselves by an odd, unusual fashion, so in language to study new phrases and affect words not in common use comes from a puerile and scholastic ambition. May I be bound to speak no other language than what is spoken in the markets of Paris! Aristophanes the grammarian was quite wrong to scold Epicurus for his plain way of delivering himself, his only aim being clarity of speech. The imitation of words, by its own ease, immediately spreads through a whole people; but the imitation of inventing and properly applying those words is much slower. The general sort of readers, having found a similar robe, mistakenly imagine they have the same body and inside too — whereas force and sinew can never be borrowed; the gloss and outward ornament, that is, words and elocution, can. Most of those I talk with speak the same language I write here, but whether they think the same thoughts I can't say. The Athenians, says Plato, study fullness and elegance of speech; the Lacedaemonians prize brevity; and those of Crete aim more at fecundity of conception than fertility of speech — and these last are the best. Zeno used to say he had two sorts of disciples: one he called philological, eager to learn things, and these were his favourites; the others, logophilic, who cared for nothing but words. Not that fine speaking isn't a very good and praiseworthy quality; but it's not so excellent and so necessary as some would make it; and I'm scandalised that our whole life should be spent in nothing else. I would first understand my own language, and that of my neighbours, with whom most of my business and conversation lies.

No doubt Greek and Latin are very great ornaments, and of very great use; but we buy them too dear. I'll set out one way, tried on my own person, by which they can be had cheaper, and anyone who wants to may make use of it. My late father, having made the most precise inquiries any man could make among men of the greatest learning and judgment for an exact method of education, was warned by them of the inconvenience then in use, and made to believe that the tedious time we spent learning the tongues of men who had them for nothing was the sole cause we couldn't reach the greatness of soul and perfection of knowledge of the ancient Greeks and Romans. I don't, however, believe that to be the only cause. So it was, that my father's expedient was this: in my infancy, before I began to speak, he committed me to the care of a German, who later died a famous physician in France, totally ignorant of our language and very fluent and a great critic in Latin. This man, whom he had fetched out of his own country and engaged with a great salary for this one purpose, had me continually with him. He had two others of lesser learning joined to him, to attend me and relieve him; they spoke to me in no language but Latin. As to the rest of the household, it was an inviolable rule that neither my father, nor my mother, nor any valet or chambermaid spoke anything in my presence but the few Latin words each had learned to gabble with me. It's not to be imagined what an advantage this proved for the whole family: my father and mother by this means learned enough Latin to understand it perfectly and to speak it well enough for any necessary use; so did those of the servants who were most often with me. In short, we Latined it at such a rate that it overflowed to all the neighbouring villages, where there still remain, established by custom, several Latin names of artisans and their tools. As for myself, I was over six years old before I understood any more French or Perigord dialect than Arabic; and without art, books, grammar, precept, whipping, or the cost of a tear, I had by that age learned to speak Latin as pure as my master's, since I had no means of mixing it with anything else. If, for example, they were to give me a theme in the college fashion, they gave it to the others in French, but to me they had to give it in bad Latin, to turn it into good. And Nicolas Grouchy, who wrote a book De Comitiis Romanorum; Guillaume Guérente, who wrote a commentary on Aristotle; George Buchanan, that great Scottish poet; and Marc-Antoine Muret (whom France and Italy have both acknowledged as the best orator of his time), my domestic tutors, all of them often told me that I had in my infancy that language so fluent and ready that they were afraid to enter into conversation with me. Buchanan in particular, whom I later saw in attendance on the late Mareschal de Brissac, then told me he was about to write a treatise on education, the example for which he intended to take from mine — for he was then tutor to that Comte de Brissac who afterwards proved so brave and valiant a gentleman.

As for Greek, of which I have only a smattering, my father also planned to have it taught me by a device — but a new one, and by way of play — tossing our declensions back and forth like those who learn geometry and arithmetic by certain games of tables. For he, among other rules, had been advised to make me relish learning and duty by an unforced will, of my own voluntary motion, and to educate my soul in all liberty and pleasure, without severity or constraint. He was an observer of this even to the point of superstition, if I may say so. Some held the opinion that it troubles and disturbs the brains of children to wake them suddenly in the morning and snatch them violently and over-hastily from sleep (in which they are much more deeply involved than we are), and so he had me wakened by the sound of some musical instrument, and was never without a musician for the purpose. By this example you may judge of the rest. This alone is enough to commend both the prudence and the affection of so good a father, who is not to be blamed if he did not reap fruits answerable to so exquisite a cultivation. Two things were the cause of this. First, a sterile and improper soil — for although I was of a strong and healthy constitution, and of a fairly sweet and tractable disposition, I was nonetheless so heavy, idle, and listless that they couldn't rouse me from my sloth, not even to get me out to play. What I saw, I saw clearly enough, and under this heavy temperament I nourished a bold imagination and opinions above my age. I had a slow wit, that would go no faster than it was led; a tardy understanding, a languishing invention, and above all, an incredible defect of memory; so it's no wonder if from all these nothing considerable could be extracted. Second, like those who, impatient of a long and steady cure, submit to every prescription and recipe, the good man — extremely anxious about failing in something he'd so wholly set his heart on — let himself at last be overruled by common opinions, which always follow their leader like a flight of cranes. Complying with the practice of the time, no longer having about him those persons he had brought out of Italy who had given him the first model of education, he sent me at six years of age to the College of Guienne, at the time the best and most flourishing in France. And there it wasn't possible to add anything to the care he took to provide me with the ablest tutors, along with every other circumstance of education, reserving also several particular rules contrary to the college practice. But for all that, it was a college still. My Latin immediately grew corrupt, and from disuse I've since lost all use of it; so this new way of education served me only to put me into the first forms at my arrival; for at thirteen, when I came out of the college, I had run through my whole course (as they call it) and, in truth, without any sort of advantage that I can honestly boast of in all that time.

The first taste I had for books came to me from the pleasure of reading the fables of Ovid's Metamorphoses; for at about seven or eight I gave up all other diversions to read them, both because this was my native language, the easiest book I was acquainted with, and because of the subject, the most suited to my age. As for Lancelot of the Lake, Amadis of Gaul, Huon of Bordeaux, and such farragoes, by which children are most delighted, I had never so much as heard their names — nor do I yet know what they contain; so strict was the discipline I was raised in. But this was enough to make me neglect the other lessons prescribed me; and there I was infinitely lucky to have to do with an understanding tutor, who knew very well how to discreetly turn a blind eye to this and other little truancies of the same nature. By this means I ran through Virgil's Aeneid, then Terence, then Plautus, then some Italian comedies, lured by the sweetness of the subject; whereas if he had been so foolish as to break me off this diversion, I really believe I'd have brought away from college nothing but a hatred of books, as almost all our young gentlemen do. But he managed the business very tactfully, seeming to take no notice, and allowing me only such time as I could steal from my regular studies — which whetted my appetite to devour those books. For the chief things my father expected from those to whom he'd entrusted my education were affability and good humour; and to tell the truth, my manners had no vice but sloth and want of mettle. The fear wasn't that I'd do ill, but that I'd do nothing; no one predicted I'd be wicked, only useless; they foresaw idleness, not malice; and it's turned out accordingly. The complaints I hear of myself are these: "He's idle, cold in the offices of friendship and family, and in public matters too detached, too disdainful." But the most pointed of them don't say, "Why has he taken such-and-such? Why hasn't he paid so-and-so?" but, "Why doesn't he part with anything? Why doesn't he give?" And I'd take it as a favour if men would expect no greater works of supererogation from me than these. But they're unjust to demand from me what I don't owe, far more rigorously than they require from others what they do owe. In condemning me to that, they spoil the gratification of the act and deprive me of the gratitude that would be my due for it; whereas the active doing of good ought to have greater value coming from my hands, since I've never been on the receiving end at all. I can dispose all the more freely of my fortune the more it is mine, and of myself the more I am my own. And yet, if I were good at making my own case, I might quite easily turn aside these reproaches and let some people understand they aren't so much offended that I don't do enough, as that I'm able to do a great deal more than I do.

Yet for all this heavy temperament, my mind, when withdrawn into itself, was not without strong movements, solid and clear judgments about objects it could comprehend, and could, unaided, digest them. But, among other things, I really do believe it would have been wholly impossible to force it into submission by violence. Shall I tell you of one faculty of my youth? I had great assurance of expression, and flexibility of voice and gesture, in playing any part I undertook to act; for before —
"Alter ab undecimo tum me vix ceperat annus,"
["I had just entered my twelfth year." — Virgil, Bucol., 39.]

— I played the chief parts in the Latin tragedies of Buchanan, Guérente, and Muret, that were performed in our College of Guienne with great dignity. Now Andreas Goveanus, our principal, in this part of his charge as in all the others, was without comparison the best of his employment in France; and I was looked on as one of the best actors. It's an exercise I don't disapprove of in young people of quality; and I've since seen our princes, after the example of some of the ancients, in person handsomely and commendably perform these exercises; it was even permitted to persons of quality to make a profession of it in Greece.
"Aristoni tragico actori rem aperit: huic et genus et fortuna honesta erant: nec ars, quia nihil tale apud Graecos pudori est, ea deformabat."

["He imparted the matter to Aristo the tragedian, a man of good family and fortune, neither of which received any blemish by that profession — nothing of that kind being reckoned a disgrace in Greece." — Livy, xxiv. 24.]

I've always considered those impertinent who condemn these entertainments, and unjust those who refuse to admit such comedians as are worth seeing into our good towns, and grudge the people that public diversion. Well-governed communities take care to assemble their citizens not only to the solemn duties of devotion but also to sports and spectacles. They find society and friendship augmented by it; and besides, can there really be allowed a more orderly and regular diversion than one performed in everyone's sight, very often in the very presence of the supreme magistrate himself? And for my part I'd think it reasonable that the prince should sometimes gratify his people at his own expense, out of paternal goodness and affection — and that in populous cities theatres should be set up for such entertainments, if only to divert them from worse and more private actions.

To return to my subject: there is nothing like luring the appetite and affections; otherwise you make nothing but so many asses laden with books. By the lash you give them their pocketful of learning to keep; whereas, to do well, you shouldn't only lodge it with them but have them marry it.

title: That it is folly to measure truth and error by our own capacity
paragraphs: It is not, perhaps, without reason that we attribute easy belief and ready persuasion to simplicity and ignorance — for I think I have heard belief compared to the impression of a seal on the soul, which is the easier to be stamped the softer and less resistant it is.
"Ut necesse est, lancem in Libra, ponderibus impositis, deprimi, sic animum perspicuis cedere."
["As the scale of the balance must give way to the weight that presses it down, so the mind yields to demonstration." — Cicero, Acad., ii. 12.]

The emptier the soul, and the less it has by way of counterweight, the more easily it gives in to the first thing pressed upon it. This is why children, the common people, women, and the sick are the readiest to be led by the ear. But, on the other hand, it is a foolish presumption to dismiss and condemn as false everything that does not strike us as probable — the ordinary vice of people who fancy themselves wiser than their neighbours. I was once one of them; and whenever I heard talk of the dead walking, of prophecies, charms, witchcraft, or any other story I had no mind to believe —
"Somnia, terrores magicos, miracula, sagas, Nocturnos lemures, portentaque Thessala,"
["Dreams, magic terrors, marvels, sorceries, Thessalian prodigies." — Horace, Ep. ii. 3, 208.]

— I would at once pity the poor people who were taken in by such nonsense. Whereas now I find that I was as much to be pitied as they. Not that experience has taught me anything to alter my earlier opinions — though curiosity has tried — but reason has shown me that to condemn anything outright as false and impossible is to set arrogant and impious limits around the will of God and the power of our mother nature, fencing them in by the bounds of my own capacity. No folly can be greater. If we give the name of monster or miracle to everything our reason cannot make sense of, how many such things are constantly before our eyes! Consider through what clouds, almost groping in the dark, our teachers lead us to the knowledge of most ordinary things, and you will see that it is custom, not understanding, that takes the strangeness out of them —
"Jam nemo, fessus saturusque videndi, Suspicere in coeli dignatur lucida templa;"
["Weary of the sight, now no one deigns to look up to heaven's lucid temples." — Lucretius, ii. 1037.]
— and that if those same things were now newly presented to us, we should find them as incredible as any, if not more.
"Si nunc primum mortalibus adsint Ex improviso, si sint objecta repente, Nil magis his rebus poterat mirabile dici, Aute minus ante quod auderent fore credere gentes."
[Lucretius, ii. 1032. The sense of the passage is given in the preceding sentence.]
A man who had never seen a river took the first one he met for the sea; and the largest examples we have come across, we treat as the outer limits nature can produce of that kind.
"Scilicet et fluvius qui non est maximus, ei'st Qui non ante aliquem majorem vidit; et ingens Arbor, homoque videtur, et omnia de genere omni Maxima quae vidit quisque, haec ingentia fingit."

["A little river seems to him, who has never seen a larger river, a mighty stream; and so with other things — a tree, a man — anything appears greatest to him that never knew a greater." — Idem, vi. 674.]
"Consuetudine oculorum assuescunt animi, neque admirantur, neque requirunt rationes earum rerum, quas semper vident."
["Things grow familiar to men's minds by being often seen; so that they neither admire nor are they inquisitive about things they daily see." — Cicero, De Natura Deor., ii. 38.]

It is the novelty, more than the size, of things that tempts us to inquire into their causes. We ought to judge nature's infinite power with more reverence, and with a fuller acknowledgment of our own ignorance and weakness. How many unlikely things are testified to by people worthy of belief? Even if we cannot bring ourselves to accept them outright, we should at least suspend judgment, for to condemn them as impossible is, by a rash presumption, to claim that we know the outer limits of what is possible. If we properly understood the difference between the impossible and the unusual — and between what runs against the order of nature and what runs against common opinion — we would obey Chilo's rule of "Ne quid nimis": neither believe too quickly nor too slowly.

When we read in Froissart that the Comte de Foix in Béarn knew, the day after, of the defeat of John, King of Castile, at Aljubarrota — and by what means he tells us he knew — we may be allowed a smile; the same for what our annals report about Pope Honorius performing the public obsequies of King Philip Augustus at Rome on the very day he died at Mantes, and ordering the like throughout Italy. These witnesses are perhaps not authoritative enough to bind us. But what about Plutarch, who, besides several examples drawn from antiquity, tells us that he himself knows for certain that under Domitian the news of Antony's defeat in Germany was published at Rome — many days' travel away — and spread through the whole world on the same day as the battle? And what about Caesar's opinion that the report often outruns the event itself? Shall we say that these simple people let themselves be taken in by the common run, because they were less clear-sighted than we are? Is there anything more delicate, more lucid, more lively than Pliny's judgment when he chooses to put it to work? Anything less affected? Leaving aside his learning, of which I make less account — in which of these qualities do any of us match him? And yet there is hardly a young schoolboy who does not catch him in untruth and pretend to set him right about the workings of nature. When we read in Bouchet the miracles wrought by the relics of St. Hilary, away with them: his standing is not enough to take from us the right to contradict him. But to condemn all such stories wholesale, out of hand, strikes me as a singular impudence. The great St. Augustine testifies that he saw a blind child recover sight at the relics of St. Gervasius and St. Protasius at Milan; a woman at Carthage cured of cancer by the sign of the cross made over her by a newly baptised woman; his close friend Hesperius driving the spirits out of his haunted house with a little earth from Our Lord's sepulchre, which earth, carried into the church, suddenly cured a paralytic; and a woman in a procession who, having touched St. Stephen's shrine with a nosegay and then rubbed her eyes with it, recovered her sight after years of blindness — among other miracles he claims to have seen with his own eyes. How do we excuse him, and the two holy bishops Aurelius and Maximinus, both of whom he names as witnesses? Are they ignorant, simple, credulous? Or malicious impostors? Is any man alive impudent enough to think himself the equal of these men in virtue, piety, learning, judgment, or any sort of perfection?
"Qui, ut rationem nullam afferrent, ipsa auctoritate me frangerent."
["Who, though they should adduce no reason, would convince me with their authority alone." — Cicero, Tusc. Quaes., i. 21.]

To dismiss what we do not understand is a presumption of great danger and consequence — to say nothing of the absurd rashness it drags after it. Once you have, by your fine understanding, set the boundaries of truth and error, and then find that you are obliged to believe stranger things than the ones you have rejected, you are already forced to abandon your boundaries. Now, what seems to me to disturb our consciences most in these religious upheavals we are living through is the way Catholics concede so much of their belief. They imagine they look moderate and wise by granting their opponents some of the points in dispute. But, quite apart from not noticing what an advantage it is to one's adversary that you begin to give ground and retreat — and how this encourages the enemy to press on — these articles they treat as harmless are sometimes of very great importance. We must either submit ourselves wholly and absolutely to the authority of our church's order, or throw off obedience to it altogether: it is not for us to decide how much obedience we owe. And from my own experience I can say this: having once given my own opinion free rein, and neglected certain disciplines of our Church that struck me as empty or strange, I later discovered, talking with learned men, that those very things rested on very solid ground and strong foundations, and that it is only stupidity and ignorance which makes us hold them in less reverence than the rest. Why do we not notice the contradictions in our own judgments — how many things were articles of faith yesterday that look like fables today? Glory and curiosity are the two scourges of the soul. The one keeps us poking our noses into everything; the other forbids us to leave anything in doubt.

title: Of friendship
paragraphs: Watching a painter who works for me, I had a mind to imitate his method. He picks the fairest spot in the middle of any wall or panel for the main picture, which he finishes with all his care and skill, and then fills the empty space around it with grotesques — odd, fantastic figures whose only charm is their variety and the extravagance of their shapes. And in truth, what are these things I scribble but grotesques and monstrous bodies, made of various parts, with no settled shape and no order, coherence, or proportion beyond what is accidental?
"Desinit in piscem mulier formosa superne."
["A fair woman in her upper form terminates in a fish." — Horace, De Arte Poetica, v. 4.]

In this second part I keep pace with my painter; but in the first and better part I fall well short of him. My powers do not stretch to undertaking a rich piece, finely finished and laid out according to art. So I have decided to borrow one from Estienne de la Boétie — one that will do honour to and adorn all the rest of my work. It is the essay he called "Voluntary Servitude"; since then, those who did not know him have aptly enough called it "Le contr'Un." He wrote it in his youth, as an exercise, in honour of liberty and against tyrants; and it has since passed through the hands of men of great learning and judgment, not without singular and well-earned praise. It is finely written, and as full as anything can be. And yet one may say with confidence that it is far below what he was capable of. If at the more mature age at which I had the happiness to know him he had taken up a project like mine and committed his thoughts to paper, we would have seen a great many rare things, very near to rivalling the best writings of antiquity. For in natural endowments especially, I know of no man comparable to him. But he left nothing behind him except this one treatise (and that too by chance — I believe he never saw it again after it first left his hands) and some notes on that famous edict of January from our civil wars, which may perhaps find a place elsewhere. These were all I could recover of what he left. He, on his deathbed, with the most affectionate remembrance, bequeathed to me his library and papers, except for the little book of his works, which I sent to the press. And I owe this particular debt to that treatise: it was the occasion of my first acquaintance with him. It was shown to me long before I had the good fortune to meet him; and the first knowledge of his name was the first cause and foundation of a friendship which we afterwards cultivated and kept up, for as long as God was pleased to leave us together, so perfect, inviolate, and entire that the like is hardly to be found in any record; and among the men of our age there is no trace of any such thing in use. So much has to come together to build such a friendship that it is a great deal if fortune brings it about once in three centuries.

There is nothing that nature seems to have inclined us to so much as society; and Aristotle says that good legislators paid more attention to friendship than to justice. Now the highest pitch of its perfection is this: for, in general, all the friendships that pleasure, profit, or public or private interest create and sustain are so much the less beautiful and generous, and so much the less true friendships, the more they mix in some other cause, design, or fruit than friendship itself. Nor do the four ancient kinds — natural, social, hospitable, sexual — either separately or together, add up to a true and perfect friendship.

That of children to parents is rather respect: friendship is nourished by exchange, and the great gap between parents and children makes that impossible — and would in fact offend the duties of nature. Not all of a father's secret thoughts are fit to be shared with his children, lest they breed an unseemly familiarity; nor can the advice and reproofs that are one of friendship's chief offices be properly given by a son to a father. There are countries where it was the custom for children to kill their fathers, and others where fathers killed their children, to prevent them from getting in each other's way in life; and the expectations of the one naturally hang on the ruin of the other. There have been great philosophers who made nothing of this tie of nature — Aristippus, for example, who, when pressed about the affection he owed his children since they had come out of him, promptly spat, saying that this had also come out of him, and that we breed lice and worms too; and the other man Plutarch tried to reconcile with his brother: "I think no more of him for coming out of the same hole." The name brother does carry a fine and pleasant sound, and for that reason he and I called each other brothers; but the tangle of interests, the division of estates, the fact that one brother's wealth means the other's poverty — all this strangely loosens and weakens the fraternal bond. Brothers pursuing fortune and advancement along the same path can hardly avoid jostling and getting in each other's way. Besides, why should that match of character, parts, and inclinations which breeds true and perfect friendships always happen to land within these family relations? Father and son may be of utterly opposite temperaments — the same for brothers: he is my son, he is my brother; but he is hot-tempered, mean, or a fool. And besides, the more these are friendships that the law and natural obligation impose on us, the less they belong to our own choice and free will; whereas voluntary liberty produces nothing more spontaneously or properly of its own than affection and friendship. Not that I have not in my own life had all that can be expected of that kind — I had the best and most indulgent father, right into his great old age, who was himself descended from a family famous and exemplary for many generations for brotherly concord:
"Et ipse Notus in fratres animi paterni."
["And I myself, known for paternal love toward my brothers." — Horace, Ode, ii. 2, 6.]
We must not bring the love we feel for women, however much it is a matter of our own choice, into the comparison, nor rank it with the others. Its fire, I admit,
"Neque enim est dea nescia nostri Qux dulcem curis miscet amaritiem,"
["Nor is the goddess unknown to me who mixes a sweet bitterness with my love." — Catullus, lxviii. 17.]

is more active, more eager, and sharper; but at the same time more headlong, fickle, restless, and inconstant — a fever subject to bouts and remissions, which has gripped only one part of us. Whereas in friendship it is a general and universal fire, but temperate and even, a steady established heat, gentle and smooth, without sting or roughness. In love it is nothing but a frantic desire for what flees from us:
"Come segue la lepre il cacciatore Al freddo, al caldo, alla montagna, al lito; Ne piu l'estima poi the presa vede; E sol dietro a chi fugge affretta il piede"

["As the hunter pursues the hare, in cold and heat, to the mountain, to the shore, and cares for it no longer once he sees it taken, and only delights in chasing what runs from him." — Ariosto, x. 7.]

Once it crosses into the territory of friendship — that is, once desires meet — it vanishes; possession destroys it, since its end is fleshly and subject to satiety. Friendship, by contrast, is enjoyed in proportion as it is desired; it only grows, is fed, and improved by enjoyment, being itself spiritual, and the soul refining itself further by practice. Beneath this perfect friendship, those passing affections had their place in me in my younger years — to say nothing of him, who himself confesses as much, too much, in his verses; so that I knew both passions, but always so distinctly that I could tell them apart, and never set them on the same footing. The first held its flight so high and bravely that it looked down with disdain on the other, fluttering far below.

As for marriage, besides being a contract whose entry only is free — its continuance being forced and obligatory, since it depends on more than our own will, and is commonly struck for other purposes — there are almost always a thousand tangles in it to be unpicked, enough to break the thread and divert the current of any lively affection. Whereas friendship has no business or traffic with anything other than itself. Moreover, to be honest, the ordinary range of women is not such as can sustain the converse and exchange that this sacred tie requires, nor do they seem to have the constancy of mind to bear the strain of so hard and lasting a bond. And no doubt, if without this barrier such a free and voluntary intimacy could be formed, in which not only souls might enjoy each other fully, but bodies too might share in the alliance — with the whole person engaged throughout — the friendship would certainly be fuller and more perfect. But there is no example of this sex having yet risen to such a pitch, and the unanimous consent of the ancient schools rules it out entirely.

That other Greek licence is rightly abhorred by our customs, and besides — because of the necessary disparity of age and difference of roles between the lovers, as they practised it — it came no closer than marriage to the perfect union and harmony we are speaking of:
"Quis est enim iste amor amicitiae? cur neque deformem adolescentem quisquam amat, neque formosum senem?"
["For what is that friendly love? why does no one love a deformed youth or a comely old man?" — Cicero, Tusc. Quaes., iv. 33.]

Nor will the very picture the Academy paints of it, as I read them, contradict me when I say this: the first frenzy that the son of Venus put into the heart of the lover at the sight of the bloom of a budding youth — to which they allowed all the brazen, passionate efforts that an immoderate ardour can produce — was founded simply on outward beauty, the false image of physical generation. It could not be founded on the soul, which was still hidden, only just beginning to emerge, and not yet ripe enough to bloom. If this frenzy seized a base spirit, the means by which it pressed its suit were rich presents, favours toward promotion, and such trumpery, all of which the Academy entirely rejects. If it seized a more generous soul, the courtship was correspondingly noble: philosophical instruction, exhortations to revere religion, to obey the laws, to die for one's country, examples of valour, prudence, and justice — the lover working to make himself acceptable through the grace and beauty of his soul, his body's beauty being long past — hoping, by this companionship of minds, to set up a firmer and more lasting contract. When such a courtship reached its goal in due season (for what they did not require in the lover, namely patience and discretion in pursuit, they strictly required in the beloved, since he had to judge of an inward beauty hard to know and hidden), then there arose in the beloved the desire for a spiritual conception by means of a spiritual beauty. This was the main thing; the bodily was incidental and secondary — the reverse of the lover's case. For this reason they preferred the beloved, maintaining that the gods preferred him too, and they greatly blame the poet Aeschylus for having, in the loves of Achilles and Patroclus, given the lover's part to Achilles, who was in the first beardless flower of his youth and the handsomest of the Greeks. After this general union, with the sovereign and worthiest part presiding, governing, and doing its proper offices, great advantages followed, they say, for both private and public life — it made up the strength and power of the countries where it prevailed, and the chief security of liberty and justice. The healthy loves of Harmodius and Aristogiton are their examples. Hence they called it sacred and divine, and held that nothing was hostile to it except the violence of tyrants and the baseness of the common people. Finally, all that can be said in favour of the Academy is that this was a love which ended in friendship — which fits well enough with the Stoic definition of love:
"Amorem conatum esse amicitiae faciendae ex pulchritudinis specie."
["Love is a desire of contracting friendship arising from the beauty of the object." — Cicero, Tusc. Quaes., vi. 34.]
I return to my own more just and true description:
"Omnino amicitiae, corroboratis jam confirmatisque, et ingeniis, et aetatibus, judicandae sunt."
["Those are only to be reputed friendships that are fortified and confirmed by judgement and the length of time." — Cicero, De Amicit., c. 20.]

What we usually call friends and friendships are nothing but acquaintances and familiarities, formed either by occasion or by design, through which a little contact happens between our souls. But in the friendship I am speaking of, souls mix and work themselves into one another so thoroughly that the seam where they first joined no longer shows. If someone pressed me for a reason why I loved him, I find I could not put it into words except by answering: because it was he, because it was I. Beyond anything I can say, there is some inexplicable and fated power that brought on this union. We had sought each other long before we met, and from the reports we heard of one another — which worked on our affections more than ordinary report has any right to do — I think it was by some secret appointment of heaven. We embraced through our names; and at our first meeting, by chance at a great civic feast, we found ourselves so taken with each other, so familiar, so bound to each other, that from that moment on nothing was so close to us as one another.
