He wrote an excellent Latin satire, since printed, in which he excuses the speed with which our understanding ripened, saying that since it was destined to be so short, having begun so late (we were both grown men, and he was a few years older), there was no time to lose, nor were we obliged to follow the example of those slow, regular friendships that require so many precautions of long preliminary conversation. Ours has no other idea than itself, and can refer only to itself: it is no one particular consideration, nor two, nor three, nor four, nor a thousand. It is some I-know-not-what quintessence of all that mixture, which seized my whole will and carried it to plunge and lose itself in his; and which, having seized his whole will, brought it back with equal accord and appetite to plunge and lose itself in mine. Lose, I can truly say — we kept back nothing for ourselves, nothing that was either his or mine.

When Laelius, in the presence of the Roman consuls, who, after sentencing Tiberius Gracchus, were prosecuting all who had had any familiarity with him, came to ask Caius Blosius, who had been Gracchus's chief friend, how much he would have done for him, and Blosius answered, "All things" — "What! all things?" said Laelius. "And what if he had ordered you to set fire to our temples?" — "He would never have ordered me that," Blosius replied. "But what if he had?" said Laelius. "I would have obeyed him," said the other. If he was as perfect a friend to Gracchus as the histories report, there was still no need to offend the consuls by so bold a confession; he might have kept his confidence in Gracchus's disposition to himself. But those who attack his answer as seditious miss the point, and do not see — as was the case — that Blosius had Gracchus's will in his pocket, both by the power of a friend and by his thorough knowledge of the man. They were more friends than citizens, more friends to each other than either enemies or friends to their country, more friends than they were friends to ambition or innovation. Having absolutely given themselves up to one another, each held the reins of the other's inclination absolutely; and if we suppose all this guided by virtue and conducted by reason — which it could not have been without — Blosius's answer was what it ought to be. If any of their actions had gone off the handle, they were not (by my measure of friendship) friends to one another, nor even to themselves. As for the rest, that answer sounds no worse than my own would, if someone asked me, "If your will should order you to kill your daughter, would you do it?" — and I answered yes. This expresses no agreement to such an act, since I have no suspicion of my own will, and as little of such a friend's. No eloquence in the world could dispossess me of my certainty about my friend's intentions and resolutions. There is not a single action of his, with whatever face it might wear, that I could not at first glance trace back to its true motive. Our souls were drawn so closely together, had regarded each other with such ardent affection and laid open the very bottom of our hearts to each other with the same affection, that I not only knew his as well as my own — in any concern of mine I would have trusted my interest more willingly with him than with myself.

Let no one therefore rank ordinary friendships with this one. I have had my share of these, like anyone else, and of the best kind of them; but I would not have anyone confuse the rules of the two, or they will fool themselves badly. In those other ordinary friendships you have to walk with bridle in hand, with prudence and watchfulness, since the knot is not sure enough that you can avoid half-suspecting it will slip. "Love him," Chilo said, "as if you were one day to hate him; and hate him as if you were one day to love him." This precept, abominable in the sovereign and perfect friendship I am speaking of, is very sensible for ordinary, everyday friendships, to which Aristotle's well-worn saying — "O my friends, there is no friend" — applies very well. In this noble commerce, the good offices, gifts, and favours by which other friendships are maintained do not even deserve mention. The reason is the merging of our wills. Just as the kindness I feel for myself is in no way increased by anything I do to relieve myself in need (whatever the Stoics say), and as I owe no debt to myself for any service I do myself, so the union of such friends, being truly perfect, takes from them all sense of such duties and makes them detest and banish from their conversation the words of division and distinction — benefit, obligation, acknowledgment, request, thanks, and the like. All things — wills, thoughts, opinions, goods, wives, children, honours, lives — being in effect common between them, and the absolute concurrence of their affections being nothing other than one soul in two bodies (in Aristotle's very apt definition), they can neither lend nor give anything to one another. This is why lawgivers, to give marriage some semblance of this divine alliance, forbid all gifts between husband and wife, implying that all should belong to each of them, and that they have nothing to divide or to give to each other.

If, in the friendship I am speaking of, one could give to the other, the receiver of the favour would be the one putting his friend in his debt. Each of them, contending above all to be useful to the other, the one who provides the opportunity is the generous one — giving his friend the satisfaction of doing for him the thing he most desires to do. When the philosopher Diogenes was short of money, he used to say that he was reclaiming it from his friends, not asking for it. To show how this works in practice, let me give you an ancient and singular example. Eudamidas, a Corinthian, had two friends: Charixenus the Sicyonian and Areteus the Corinthian. Coming to die poor, while his two friends were rich, he made his will in this fashion: "I bequeath to Areteus the keeping of my mother, to provide for her in her old age; and to Charixenus I bequeath the task of marrying my daughter, and giving her as good a dowry as he is able; and should one of these die first, I substitute the survivor in his place." The first to see the will laughed at it, but the legatees, when they heard, accepted it with very great content. One of them, Charixenus, died five days later; the whole charge now falling on Areteus, he took care of the old woman with great affection, and out of the five talents he had to his name he gave two and a half as dowry for his own only daughter, and two and a half as dowry for Eudamidas's daughter, and held both weddings on the same day.

This example is quite complete — except for one objection: the multitude of friends. For the perfect friendship I am speaking of is indivisible. Each gives himself so entirely to his friend that nothing is left to share around. On the contrary, he is sorry he is not double, treble, quadruple, that he has not many souls and many wills to lavish them all on this one object. Ordinary friendships admit of division: one may love the beauty in this person, the good humour in that, the generosity of a third, the paternal affection of a fourth, the brotherly love of a fifth, and so on. But this friendship, which takes possession of the whole soul and rules and sways there with absolute sovereignty, simply cannot admit of a rival. If two were to call on you for help at the same moment, to which would you run? If they required opposite services of you, how would you serve them both? If one entrusted you with a secret that it mattered to the other to know, how would you find your way out? A unique and particular friendship dissolves every other obligation: the secret I have sworn not to reveal to any other, I may, without breaking my word, share with him who is not another, but myself. It is miracle enough for a man to double himself; and those who talk of tripling do not know what they are saying. Nothing is extreme that has its like; and whoever supposes that out of two friends I love one as much as the other, that they love each other and love me as much as I love them, is multiplying into a brotherhood the most singular of units — of which, moreover, even one alone is the hardest thing in the world to find. The rest of the story fits nicely with what I was saying. For Eudamidas, as a benefaction and favour, bequeathes to his friends a legacy of being employed in his need; he leaves them heirs to his own generosity, which consists in giving them the chance of doing him a kindness. And no doubt the force of friendship shows more clearly in his act than in Areteus's. In short, these are effects that cannot be pictured or grasped except by those who have lived them, and which make me infinitely admire the answer of that young soldier to Cyrus, who, when asked how much he would take for a horse with which he had won a race, and whether he would exchange him for a kingdom, replied, "No, truly, sir, but I would give him with all my heart, to get thereby a true friend, could I find any man worthy of that alliance." He spoke well in saying "could I find": for although one can almost anywhere come across men suitable for a surface acquaintance, where a man has to deal from the very bottom of his heart, with no reservation whatever, all the springs and tumblers have to be truly cut and perfectly true.

In partnerships that hold by only one tie, we only have to guard against the failings that concern that one tie. It is no business of mine what religion my doctor or my lawyer is — that has nothing to do with the offices of friendship they owe me; and I take the same indifferent view of the household business my servants do with me. I never ask, when I take on a footman, whether he is chaste, only whether he is diligent; I am not anxious whether my muleteer is a gambler, but whether he is strong and able; or whether my cook swears, but whether he is a good cook. I do not pretend to dictate what others should do in running their households — there are plenty who interfere enough with that — I only give an account of my own way:
"Mihi sic usus est: tibi, ut opus est facto, face."
["This has been my way; as for you, do as you find needful." — Terence, Heaut., i. 1, 28.]

For table-talk I prefer the pleasant and witty over the learned and the grave; in bed, beauty over goodness; in everyday talk, the ablest speaker, sincere or not. And just as that man who was caught astride a hobby-horse playing with his children begged the person who had surprised him not to say anything until he himself was a father — supposing that the fondness which would then fill his own soul would make him a fairer judge of such an act — so I would wish to speak with people who have experienced what I am describing. But knowing how far such a friendship is from common practice, and how rare it is to be found, I despair of meeting any such judge. Even the writings antiquity has left us on this subject seem to me flat and weak compared with the sense I have of it. In this matter, the facts go beyond the precepts of philosophy.
"Nil ego contulerim jucundo sanus amico."
["While I have sense left to me, there will never be anything more acceptable to me than an agreeable friend." — Horace, Sat., i. 5, 44.]

The ancient Menander said that the man who had the good fortune to meet with even the shadow of a friend was happy. And he had good reason to say so, especially if he spoke from experience. For in good earnest, if I compare the rest of my life — though, thanks be to God, I have spent my time pleasantly and at ease, free, apart from the loss of such a friend, from any grievous affliction, in great tranquillity of mind, content with my natural and original advantages without straining after others — if I compare it all, I say, with the four years I had the happiness to enjoy the sweet company of this excellent man, it is nothing but smoke, an obscure and tedious night. From the day that I lost him —
"Quern semper acerbum, Semper honoratum (sic, di, voluistis) habebo,"
["A day for me ever sad, for ever sacred, so have you willed, ye gods." — Aeneid, v. 49.]

— I have only led a languishing life; and even the pleasures that come my way, instead of giving me comfort, double my grief at his loss. We were halves of each other throughout, and to such a degree that by outliving him, I feel I am cheating him of his share.
"Nec fas esse ulla me voluptate hic frui Decrevi, tantisper dum ille abest meus particeps."
["I have determined that it will never be right for me to enjoy any pleasure, so long as he, with whom I shared all pleasures, is away." — Terence, Heaut., i. 1, 97.]
I had grown so used to being always his double, in every place and in everything, that it seems to me I am no more than half of myself:
"Illam meae si partem anima tulit Maturior vis, quid moror altera? Nec carus aeque, nec superstes Integer? Ille dies utramque Duxit ruinam."

If that half of my soul were snatched away from me by an untimely stroke, why should the other stay? What remains will not be equally dear, will not be whole: the same day will involve the destruction of both.
or:

["If a superior force has taken that part of my soul, why do I, the remaining one, linger behind? What is left is not so dear, nor an entire thing: this day has wrought the destruction of both." — Horace, Ode, ii. 17, 5.]

There is no action or thought of mine in which I do not miss him, just as I know he would have missed me. For just as he exceeded me by infinite degrees in virtue and every other accomplishment, so he did in the duties of friendship:
"Quis desiderio sit pudor, aut modus Tam cari capitis?"
["What shame can there be, or measure, in lamenting so dear a friend?" — Horace, Ode, i. 24, 1.]

"O misero frater adempte mihi! Omnia tecum una perierunt gaudia nostra, Quae tuus in vita dulcis alebat amor. Tu mea, tu moriens fregisti commoda, frater; Tecum una tota est nostra sepulta anima Cujus ego interitu tota de menthe fugavi Haec studia, atque omnes delicias animi. Alloquar? audiero nunquam tua verba loquentem? Nunquam ego te, vita frater amabilior Aspiciam posthac; at certe semper amabo;"

["O brother, taken from me miserable! With thee, all our joys have vanished, the joys that, in thy life, thy dear love nourished. Dying, thou, my brother, hast destroyed all my happiness. My whole soul is buried with thee. Through whose death I have banished from my mind these studies, and all the delights of the mind. Shall I address thee? I shall never hear thy voice. Never shall I behold thee hereafter. O brother, dearer to me than life. Nothing remains, but assuredly I shall ever love thee." — Catullus, lxviii. 20; lxv.]
But let us hear a boy of sixteen speak:

"Because I have learned that that work has since been brought out, with a mischievous design, by those bent on disturbing and changing the state of our government, without bothering to consider whether they are likely to improve it; and because they have mixed his work up with some of their own writing, I have refrained from including it here. But so that the memory of its author may not suffer with those who could not come close enough to know his principles, I want them to understand that he wrote it in his boyhood, by way of exercise only, as a common theme that has been worked over by a thousand writers. I do not doubt that he believed what he wrote, being so conscientious that he would not lie even in jest; and what is more, I know that if it had been his own choice, he would rather have been born in Venice than in Sarlat — and with reason. But he had another maxim sovereignly impressed on his soul: to obey and submit very religiously to the laws under which he was born. There never was a better citizen, more affectionate to his country; nor a greater enemy to all the commotions and innovations of his time — so that he would much rather have used his talents to put out those civil flames than to add any fuel to them; his mind was modelled on better ages. Now, in exchange for this serious piece, I will give you another, in a more gay and frolicsome vein, from the same hand, written at the same age."

title: Nine and twenty sonnets of Estienne de la Boitie
paragraphs: TO MADAME DE GRAMMONT, COMTESSE DE GUISSEN.
[They contain little more than lover's complaints, expressed in a rather rough style, full of the follies and outbursts of a restless passion, gorged with jealousies, fears, and suspicions. — Coste.]

[These — included in the 1588 edition — were twenty-nine sonnets of La Boétie, accompanied by a dedicatory epistle to Madame de Grammont. The sonnets, referred to at the end of Chapter XXVII, do not really belong to the book, and are of only slight interest now; the epistle has been transferred to the Correspondence. The sonnets, with the letter, were presumably sent some time after Letters V and following. Montaigne seems to have had several copies written out to forward to friends or acquaintances.]

title: Of moderation
paragraphs: As if we had an infectious touch, we corrupt by our handling things that in themselves are good and praiseworthy. We can grip virtue so tightly that it turns vicious, if we embrace it too narrowly and with too violent a desire. Those who say there can never be excess in virtue, since once it becomes excess it ceases to be virtue, are merely playing with words:
"Insani sapiens nomen ferat, aequus iniqui, Ultra quam satis est, virtutem si petat ipsam."
["Let the wise man bear the name of a madman, the just one of an unjust, if he seek wisdom more than is sufficient." — Horace, Ep., i. 6, 15.]
The wise man is no longer wise, the just man no longer just, if he seek to carry his love for wisdom or virtue beyond what is necessary.

This is a subtle point of philosophy. A man may both love virtue too much and be excessive in a just act. Holy Writ agrees: "Be not wiser than you should, but be soberly wise." I have known a great man

damage the reputation he had for piety by aiming at a devotion beyond anything ever seen in others of his rank. I love temperate and moderate natures. An immoderate zeal, even toward what is good, astonishes me even when it does not offend, and leaves me at a loss what to call it. Neither the mother of Pausanias,

who was the first to start the case against her son and threw the first stone toward his death, nor Postumius the dictator, who put his son to death because in the heat of youth he had successfully charged the enemy a little ahead of the rest of his squadron, strike me as so much just as strange; and I would neither advise nor like to follow so savage a virtue, that costs so dear.

The archer who shoots over the mark misses just as much as one who shoots short; and it is equally hard on my sight to look up at a great light and to look down into a dark abyss. Callicles in Plato says that the furthest reaches of philosophy are harmful, and advises against diving into it beyond the point where it pays off. Taken moderately, he says, it is pleasant and useful, but pushed too far it leaves a man brutish and vicious, scornful of religion and the common laws, an enemy to civil society and to all human pleasures, useless for any public office, unable to help others or even himself, and a ready target for every kind of insult and injury. He is right. In its excess, philosophy enslaves our natural freedom, and through some impertinent subtlety it leads us off the fair, beaten path that nature has marked out for us.

The love we feel for our wives is entirely lawful, and yet theology thinks it right to keep it in check. I recall reading somewhere in St. Thomas Aquinas a condemnation of marriages within the forbidden degrees, with this among his reasons: there is some danger that the friendship a man feels for such a woman will become immoderate; for if the conjugal affection is full and perfect between them, as it ought to be, and is then further loaded with the affection of kinship, there is no doubt the husband will be carried beyond the bounds of reason.

Those sciences that regulate men's manners — theology and philosophy — will have their say in everything. There is no act so private and secret that it can escape their inspection and jurisdiction. The best instructed are those who are most able to control and curb their own freedom; women will expose themselves freely for pleasure, though when it comes to medical necessity they are as shy as can be. In their behalf, then, I will

teach husbands — those, that is, who are too vehement in marital exercise, if such still exist — this lesson: that even the pleasures they enjoy in the society of their wives are blameable if immoderate, and that a wanton and riotous abuse of them is just as reprovable here as in illicit affairs. Those indecent and lewd tricks and postures that first passion suggests are not only indecently but harmfully practised on our wives. Let them learn impudence from some other source; they are always ready enough for what we need from them, and for my own part, I have always gone the plain way to work.

Marriage is a solemn, religious tie, and so the pleasure we draw from it should be a sober and serious delight, mixed with a certain gravity — a discreet, conscientious sort of pleasure. And since its chief end is generation, some have questioned whether, when men are out of hope of children — too old, or when the wife is already pregnant — it is lawful to embrace our wives. It is homicide, according to Plato. Certain nations — the Mohammedan among others — abhor any union with women who are pregnant; others, with women who are in their courses. Zenobia would let her husband in only for a single encounter, after which she sent him off to manage his own appetites for the whole period of her conception, and only after that would receive him again — a brave and generous example of conjugal continence. It was, no doubt, from some lascivious poet, himself in great straits for a little of this sport, that Plato borrowed the story that Jupiter was once so hot for his wife that, not having the patience to wait for the couch, he threw her down on the floor, where the violence of pleasure made him forget the great and important decisions he had just taken with the other gods in their heavenly council, and made him boast that he had had as good a time of it as when, unknown to her parents, he first took her maidenhead.

The kings of Persia used to invite their wives to the start of their feasts; but once the wine had really begun to work, and they meant to give pleasure its head, they sent them back to their private quarters, so that they would not have to take part in their immoderate lust, sending in other women in their stead, with whom they were not bound by the same decorum. Not all pleasures and all forms of gratification fit all persons. Epaminondas had put a young man in prison for certain debaucheries; when Pelopidas pleaded that, at his request, the young man might be released, Epaminondas refused; but he granted it at once, at the first word, to a wench of his who made the same plea — saying that this was a favour fit for one such as she, but not for a general. Sophocles, joint praetor with Pericles, happened to see a fine boy go by and exclaimed, "What a charming boy!" "That might do very well," answered Pericles, "for someone other than a praetor, who must keep not only his hands but his eyes chaste." The emperor Aelius Verus answered his wife, who reproached him with his love of other women, that he did it on a conscientious account, since marriage was a name of honour and dignity, not of wanton and lascivious desire; and our church history preserves with great reverence the memory of a woman who left her husband because she would not yield to his indecent and inordinate desires. In short, there is no pleasure so just and lawful that intemperance and excess in it should not be condemned.

But, to speak the truth, isn't man a wretched creature on this score? It is scarcely within his nature to taste a single pleasure pure and entire; and yet he sets up doctrines and precepts to cut down the little he has — he is not yet wretched enough, unless by art and study he can add to his own misery.
"Fortunae miseras auximus arte vias."
["We artificially augment the wretchedness of fortune." — Propertius, iii. 7, 44.]

Human wisdom misuses its talent as much when it sets to work cutting down the number and sweetness of the pleasures that are naturally our due, as it uses it well when it artfully dresses up and disguises the ills of life to soften the feel of them. Had I been in charge, I would have taken another, more natural course — one which, to tell the truth, is both convenient and holy, and which perhaps I could have set within bounds. But our spiritual and bodily physicians, as if by mutual agreement, can find no other way to cure the body's and the soul's infirmities than by misery and pain. To this end, vigils, fasts, hair-shirts, distant and solitary banishments, perpetual imprisonments, scourges, and other afflictions have been introduced — but on the understanding that they will sting, that they will be real afflictions; not turn out as they did with one Gallio, who, having been exiled to Lesbos, was soon reported back in Rome to be living merry as the day is long, and that what had been laid on him as a penance had turned to his pleasure. The Senate then thought fit to recall him home to his wife and family, and confine him to his own house, in order to suit the punishment to his actual feelings. To the man whom fasting makes more healthful and more lively, and to the man whose palate prefers fish to flesh, the prescription of these would have no curative effect — any more than drugs swallowed with appetite and pleasure cure the patient. The bitterness of the potion and the patient's aversion are necessary for the cure to work. The nature that would eat rhubarb like buttered turnips would frustrate the use and virtue of it; it must be something to trouble and disturb the stomach, that must purge and cure it. And here the common rule — that contraries cure — fails, for in this one case ill is cured by ill.

This belief somewhat resembles the other very ancient one, that the gods and nature could be gratified by massacre and murder — an opinion once universally received in all religions. And even in the late times within our fathers' memory, Amurath, on taking the Isthmus, sacrificed six hundred young Greeks to his father's soul as a propitiatory offering for his sins. And in the new lands discovered in our age, still pure and virgin compared with ours, this practice is in some measure everywhere received: their idols all reek with human blood, with various instances of horrid cruelty. Some they burn alive, taking them half-broiled off the coals to tear out their hearts and entrails; some — even women — they flay alive and use the bloody skins to clothe and disguise others. Nor are we without striking examples of constancy and resolve in this business: the poor souls who are to be sacrificed — old men, women, and children — themselves going around some days before to beg alms for their own sacrifice, then presenting themselves to the slaughter, singing and dancing with the spectators.

The ambassadors of the king of Mexico, in setting out for Fernando Cortez the power and greatness of their master, said that he had thirty vassals each capable of raising a hundred thousand fighting men, that he held court in the fairest and best-fortified city under the sun, and added at last that he was obliged each year to offer fifty thousand men to the gods. They also said he maintained a continual war with some powerful neighbouring nations, not only to keep the young men in training, but principally to have prisoners of war to supply his sacrifices. At a certain town elsewhere, in welcome to Cortez, they sacrificed fifty men at once. I will tell one more such tale and be done. Some of these people, beaten by Cortez, sent to acknowledge him and treat with him for peace, and their messengers brought three sorts of gifts, which they presented in these terms: "Behold, lord, here are five slaves: if you are a fierce god that feeds on flesh and blood, eat these, and we will bring you more; if you are a kindly god, here is incense and feathers; but if you are a man, take these fowls and these fruits that we have brought you."

title: Of cannibals
paragraphs: When King Pyrrhus invaded Italy, after surveying the order of the army the Romans had sent out to meet him, he said: "I do not know what kind of barbarians these may be" — for so the Greeks called all other nations — "but the disposition of this army that I see before me has nothing barbarous in it." The Greeks said as much of the army Flaminius brought into their country; and Philip, watching from a height the order and lay-out of the Roman camp Publius Sulpicius Galba had pitched in his kingdom, made a similar remark. By which it appears how careful men ought to be of taking things on trust from common opinion, and that we ought to judge with the eye of reason, not by common report.

I long had a man living in my house who had spent ten or twelve years in the New World, in the part of it where Villegaignon landed and which he called Antarctic France. This discovery of so vast a country seems to me a thing of very great importance. I cannot be sure that no other will be made in the future, given how many wiser men than ourselves have been mistaken about this one. I am afraid our eyes are bigger than our bellies, and that we have more curiosity than capacity; we grasp at everything and end up holding only wind.

Plato has Solon tell a story he had heard from the priests of Sais in Egypt: that long ago, before the Flood, there was a great island called Atlantis, lying directly at the mouth of the Strait of Gibraltar, larger than Africa and Asia put together; that its kings ruled not only that island but also extended their dominion far into the continent — holding a portion of Africa as far as Egypt, and in Europe as far as Tuscany — and that they tried to push as well into Asia, subjugating all the nations bordering the Mediterranean as far as the Black Sea. To this end they overran all Spain, Gaul, and Italy, and pressed on into Greece, where the Athenians stopped them. But some time afterwards both the Athenians, and the islanders and their island, were swallowed by the Flood.
It is very likely that this enormous burst and inundation of water worked wonderful changes in the layout of the earth — as it is said that the sea then divided Sicily from Italy:
"Haec loca, vi quondam et vasta convulsa ruina, Dissiluisse ferunt, quum protenus utraque tellus Una foret"
["These lands, they say, formerly with violence and vast desolation convulsed, burst asunder, where erewhile were." — Aeneid, iii. 414.]
Cyprus from Syria, the island of Negropont from the continent of Boeotia; and elsewhere it joined lands that had been separate before, filling in the channel between them with sand and mud:
"Sterilisque diu palus, aptaque remis, Vicinas urbes alit, et grave sentit aratrum."
["That which was once a sterile marsh, and bore vessels on its bosom, now feeds neighbouring cities, and admits the plough." — Horace, De Arte Poetica, v. 65.]

But there is no real likelihood that this island was the New World so recently discovered: that almost touched Spain, and it would be an incredible feat of any flood to have thrown so prodigious a mass back more than twelve hundred leagues. Besides, our modern navigators have nearly established that it is no island but mainland, joined with the East Indies on one side, and with the lands under the two poles on the other; or, if it is separated from them, by so narrow a strait that it hardly deserves the name of an island on that account.

It seems that in this great body of the earth there are two sorts of motion, as in our own — one natural and the other feverish. When I think of the impression our river, the Dordogne, has made in my time on its right bank, how in twenty years it has gained so much ground and undermined the foundations of so many houses, I take it for an unusual agitation; for if it had always run that way, or were to do so in future, the look of the world would be wholly changed. But rivers alter their course, beating now against one bank, now the other, and sometimes keeping quietly to their channel. I am not speaking of sudden floods, the causes of which everyone understands. In Médoc, by the seashore, my brother, Sieur d'Arsac, sees an estate he owned there buried under the sands that the sea throws up before it; the tops of some houses are still to be seen, and his rents and lands have been turned into pitiful, barren scrub. The people of the place say that of late years the sea has been driving so hard against them that they have lost more than four leagues of land. These sands are her outriders, and we can now see great mounds of moving sand marching half a league ahead of her, taking the land as they go.

The other testimony from antiquity to which some would tie this discovery of the New World is in Aristotle — at any rate, if that little book on Marvellous Things Heard is his. He tells us there that certain Carthaginians, having crossed the Atlantic beyond the Strait of Gibraltar and sailed a very long time, at last came upon a great and fruitful island, all covered with wood and watered by several broad and deep rivers, lying far from any mainland; and that they, and others after them, drawn by the goodness and fertility of the soil, went there with their wives and children and began to plant a colony. But the Carthaginian senate, seeing their own people slowly diminishing in numbers, issued an express order on pain of death that no one should travel there, and drove out these new settlers — fearing, it is said, that in time the colony would so multiply as to supplant and ruin the home state. But this report of Aristotle's no more agrees with our new-found lands than the other.

The man I had was plain and ignorant, and so all the likelier to tell the truth — for your better-bred sort of men are sharper observers, true, and see more; but then they gloss over what they see, and, to give greater weight to what they tell you and win your belief, they cannot keep from tweaking the story a little. They never report things to you simply as they are, but as they appeared to them, or as they want them to appear to you; and to win a reputation for sound judgment, and to gain your trust, they are happy to help the case along with something more than is strictly true, of their own invention. What we need, in such a case, is either a man of unimpeachable honesty, or one so simple that he has nothing in him with which to dress up false stories and give them a colour of truth, and no axe to grind in fabricating. Mine was such a man; and besides, he has at various times brought me sailors and merchants who had made the same voyage at the same time. So I will content myself with his testimony, without bothering about what the cosmographers say. We should have topographers to map out for us the particular places they have actually been; but having had this advantage over us — of having seen the Holy Land — they think they have the right, naturally, to tell us stories about every other part of the world besides. I would have every man write down what he knows, and as much as he knows, but no more — and not just on this subject but on every other. For someone may have particular knowledge or experience of some river or fountain, who otherwise knows no more than anyone else, and yet, to get a circulation for his little hoard of learning, will undertake to write a whole book on physics. From this vice large mischiefs grow.

Now, to come back to my subject: from anything I can gather, there is nothing barbarous or savage about that nation, except that everyone calls barbarism whatever is not in use in his own country. Indeed, we have no other measure of truth and reason than the example and pattern of the opinions and customs of the place where we live: there is always the perfect religion, there the perfect government, there the most accomplished and proper usage of everything. They are savages in the same sense that we call fruits wild when they have grown of themselves, by nature's own ordinary course; whereas in truth we should rather call those wild whose nature we have changed by our artifice, and diverted from the common order. In the first sort the genuine, most useful, and natural virtues and properties are vigorous and lively, which in the others we have helped to corrupt by adjusting them to suit our corrupted palate. And yet even our taste can find a flavour and delicacy, beyond what we can match, in some of the fruits those countries produce without art or cultivation. It is not reasonable that art should win the prize over our great and powerful mother nature. We have so smothered the beauty and richness of her own work with the extra ornaments and graces of our invention that we have very nearly stifled her — yet in other places, where she shines in her own purity and proper lustre, she shames our vain and trivial efforts in the most striking way:
"Et veniunt hederae sponte sua melius; Surgit et in solis formosior arbutus antris; Et volucres nulls dulcius arte canunt."
["The ivy grows best spontaneously, the arbutus best in shady caves; and the wild notes of birds are sweeter than art can teach." — Propertius, i. 2, 10.]
Our best efforts cannot even imitate the nest of the least of birds — its make, its beauty, its convenience — or even a poor spider's web.
All things, Plato says, are produced either by nature, by chance, or by art; the greatest and finest by one or the other of the first two, the least and least perfect by the last.

These nations, then, seem to me barbarous only in this: that they have taken on so little stamp from human art and invention, and so are still very close to their original simplicity. The laws of nature still govern them, hardly contaminated by ours; and that in such purity that I am sometimes sorry we did not come to know them sooner, in those better ages when there were men more capable of judging them than we are. I am sorry that Lycurgus and Plato had no knowledge of them; for, to my mind, what we see now in these nations not only surpasses all the pictures with which the poets have decked out the golden age, and all their inventions in imagining a happy state of mankind, but it goes beyond the imagination and even the wish and longing of philosophy itself. So native and pure a simplicity as we see by experience to exist in them could never have entered the philosophers' minds, nor could they have believed that human society could be maintained with so little artifice and so little human patching. I would tell Plato that this is a nation with no sort of trade, no knowledge of letters, no science of numbers, no name for magistrate or political authority, no use of slavery, no riches or poverty, no contracts, no inheritances, no shares, no occupations except leisure, no respect of kinship beyond the common, no clothing, no agriculture, no metal, no use of corn or wine — the very words for lying, treachery, dissimulation, avarice, envy, slander, pardon, unheard of.
How short would he find his imaginary republic of this perfection?
"Viri a diis recentes."
["Men fresh from the gods." — Seneca, Ep., 90.]
"Hos natura modos primum dedit."
["These were the manners first taught by nature." — Virgil, Georgics, ii. 20.]

As for the rest, they live in a country that is very pleasant and temperate, so that, as my witnesses tell me, it is rare to hear of anyone falling ill, and they assure me they have never seen any of the natives palsied, bleary-eyed, toothless, or bent with age. The country lies along the seashore, fenced on the inland side by great high mountains, with a stretch of about a hundred leagues between. They have plenty of fish and meat, none of which look like ours, and they eat them with no cookery beyond plain boiling, roasting, and grilling. The first man to ride in there on a horse, though in earlier voyages he had become acquainted and familiar with them, frightened them so badly with his centaur appearance that they killed him with their arrows before they could make out who he was. Their houses are very long, big enough to hold two or three hundred people, made of the bark of tall trees, one end stuck in the ground and the trees leaning on each other at the top to support one another, like some of our barns, where the roof comes right down to the ground and serves as side walls too. They have wood so hard that they cut with it and make their swords from it, and grills from it to grill their meat. Their beds are of cotton, slung from the roof like our sailors' hammocks, every man with his own — for the wives sleep apart from their husbands. They rise with the sun, and as soon as they are up, eat for the whole day, since they have no further meals. They do not drink at meals — as Suidas reports of certain other peoples of the East who never drank with their food — but drink very often during the rest of the day, and sometimes to a rousing pitch. Their drink is made of a certain root and is the colour of our claret, and they only ever drink it lukewarm. It keeps no more than two or three days; it has a slightly sharp, brisk taste, is not at all heady, but very kind to the stomach; laxative to strangers but a pleasant beverage to those used to it. Instead of bread they use a certain white compound, like coriander seeds; I have tasted it — the flavour is sweet and a little bland. The whole day is spent in dancing. The young men go off to hunt wild beasts with bows and arrows; meanwhile some of the women are busy heating their drink, which is their chief occupation. One of their old men, in the morning before they begin to eat, preaches to the whole household, walking from one end of the house to the other and repeating the same sentence over and over until he has completed the round — for their houses are at least a hundred yards long. Valour against their enemies and love toward their wives are the two heads of his sermon, never failing to remind them, in closing, that it is their wives who give them their drink warm and well-seasoned. The shape of their beds, ropes, swords, the wooden bracelets they tie around their wrists when they go to fight, and the great canes hollowed out at one end, by whose sound they keep the cadence of their dances, are to be seen in several places, and among them at my house. They shave themselves all over, and much more neatly than we do, with no razor but one of wood or stone. They believe in the immortality of the soul, and that those who have deserved well of the gods are lodged in that part of heaven where the sun rises, and the damned in the west.

They have I do not know what kind of priests and prophets, who very rarely appear in public, living up in the mountains. When one of them arrives there is a great feast and a solemn assembly of several villages — each house, as I have described, makes a village, and they are about a French league apart. This prophet speaks publicly to the people, urging them to virtue and duty; but all their ethics come down to two articles: resoluteness in war, and devotion to their wives. He also prophesies to them the events to come and the outcomes they may expect from their enterprises, and pushes them toward war or away from it. But he had better look out: if he fails in his prediction, and anything turns out otherwise than he foretold, he is hacked into a thousand pieces if he is caught, and condemned as a false prophet. For that reason, any of them who has been wrong once is heard from no more.

Divination is a gift of God, and so to abuse it ought to be a punishable imposture. Among the Scythians, when their diviners failed to deliver what they had promised, they were bound hand and foot, laid on carts loaded with brushwood and faggots, drawn along by oxen, and burned alive. Those who deal only with matters within the reach of human capacity are excusable in doing the best they can. But those others, who come to swindle us with claims of an extraordinary faculty beyond our understanding — ought they not to be punished when they fail to make good their promise, and for the rashness of their imposture?

They are continually at war with the nations who live further inland, beyond their mountains, to which they go naked, with no other weapons than their bows and wooden swords, shaped at one end like the head of our javelins. The obstinacy of their battles is something wonderful, and they never end without much loss of blood — for as for running away, they do not know what that is. Each one brings home, for a trophy, the head of an enemy he has killed, and fixes it over the door of his house. After treating their prisoners very well for a long time, and giving them every delicacy they can think of, the man to whom the prisoner belongs invites a great gathering of his friends. When they are all assembled, he ties a rope to one of the prisoner's arms, holding the other end himself at a distance out of his reach, and gives his closest friend the other arm to hold in the same way; and then the two of them, in front of the whole assembly, dispatch the prisoner with their swords. After that they roast him, eat him among themselves, and send some morsels to absent friends. They do not do this, as some have supposed, for nourishment — as the Scythians anciently did — but as the ultimate token of revenge. This appears from the following: having seen that the Portuguese, who were allied to their enemies, inflicted a different sort of death on prisoners they took — burying them up to the waist, shooting arrows at the upper part until it bristled with them, and then hanging them — they assumed that these people from another world, who had spread the knowledge of many vices to their neighbours and were far greater masters of every sort of mischief than they were, must have a reason for adopting this kind of revenge, and that it must be more painful than their own; so they began to drop their old way and follow this one. I am not so much sorry that we should note the barbarous horror of so cruel a deed, as that, while we see their faults so plainly, we are so blind to our own. I take it that there is more barbarity in eating a man alive than in eating him dead; in tearing apart by racks and torments a body still in full sensation; in roasting it by degrees, in having it bitten and worried to death by dogs and pigs (as we have not only read about, but lately seen — not between sworn and mortal enemies, but between neighbours and fellow-citizens, and, what is worse, under the colour of piety and religion) — than to roast and eat him after he is dead.

Chrysippus and Zeno, the two heads of the Stoic school, thought there was no harm in using our dead bodies in whatever way we needed, even for food — as our own ancestors did, when, besieged by Caesar in the city of Alesia, they decided to keep themselves alive during the siege on the bodies of their old men, women, and others unfit to bear arms.
"Vascones, ut fama est, alimentis talibus usi Produxere animas."
["It is said the Gascons with such meats appeased their hunger." — Juvenal, Sat., xv. 93.]

And our physicians make no bones about putting it to all sorts of uses, applying it either outwardly or giving it inwardly, for the health of the patient. But no opinion has ever been so out of bounds as to excuse treachery, disloyalty, tyranny, and cruelty — which are our familiar vices. So we may indeed call these people barbarous as judged by the rules of reason, but not as judged against ourselves, who outdo them in every kind of barbarity. Their wars are throughout noble and generous, and have as much excuse and fair pretext as that human plague is capable of: their sole motive is the rivalry of valour. Their disputes are not over new territory — what they already have is so fruitful by nature that it supplies them, without labour or worry, with everything they need in such abundance that they have no use for enlarging their borders. They are still at that happy stage where they want only as much as their natural needs require; everything beyond that is, for them, superfluous. Men of the same age commonly call one another brothers, the younger ones children, and the old men are fathers to all. The old leave their goods to their heirs in common possession, without any division or any other title than what nature gives her creatures in bringing them into the world. If their neighbours cross the mountains to attack them and win the day, all the victors gain is glory and the advantage of having shown themselves the better in valour and virtue. They never meddle with the goods of the conquered, but go straight home to their own country, where they want for nothing they need — and not for that greatest of goods either, the knowledge of how to enjoy their condition happily and be content. The other side, in turn, does the same. They demand no other ransom of their prisoners than the acknowledgment that they have been defeated; but you will not find one in a generation who will not rather choose to die than make such a confession, or in any word or look fall short of the full grandeur of an undefeated courage. There is not one of them who would not rather be killed and eaten than so much as open his mouth to plead that he might not be. Their captors treat them with all liberality and freedom, to make their lives that much dearer to them — but frequently bring up the subject of their approaching death, the torments they are to suffer, the preparations being made for them, the carving up of their limbs, and the feast at which their carcass will be the only dish. All this they do for one end only: to wring some soft or submissive word from them, or so to frighten them as to make them run off, in order to gain the advantage of having scared them and shaken their constancy. And in fact, if you look at it rightly, that is the only point on which true victory turns:
"Victoria nulla est, Quam quae confessor animo quoque subjugat hostes."
["No victory is complete which the conquered do not admit to be so." — Claudian, De Sexto Consulatu Honorii, v. 248.]

The Hungarians, a very warlike people, never push further than reducing the enemy to surrender; once that confession has been wrung from them, they let them go without injury or ransom — except, at most, to bind them by their word never to take up arms against them again. We have plenty of advantages over our enemies that are borrowed, not really our own. To have stronger arms and legs is a porter's quality, not the effect of virtue; to draw oneself up in formation is a dead, corporeal quality; it is a turn of fortune that makes an enemy stumble or dazzles him with the sun; it is a trick of science and craft, possible even in a base man, to be a good fencer. The worth and value of a man lies in the heart and in the will: there is his real honour. Valour is steadiness, not of legs and arms, but of courage and soul; it does not consist in the goodness of our horse or our weapons, but in our own. He who stays firm in his courage —
"Si succiderit, de genu pugnat"
["If his legs fail him, he fights on his knees." — Seneca, De Providentia, c. 2.]

— he who gives up nothing of his self-possession in the face of imminent death, who dying still throws his enemy a fierce and disdainful look, is overcome not by us but by fortune; he is killed, not conquered. The most valiant are sometimes the most unfortunate. There are defeats more triumphant than victories. Those four sister victories — the fairest the sun ever looked on, of Salamis, Plataea, Mycale, and Sicily — never dared to set their united glory against the single glory of the rout of King Leonidas and his men at the pass of Thermopylae. Who ever ran with a more glorious purpose, a higher ambition, toward winning a battle than Captain Iscolas did toward the certain loss of one? Who could have come up with a more subtle device to secure his own safety than he found to assure his own destruction? He was sent to defend a certain pass of the Peloponnese against the Arcadians; finding it utterly impossible, given the lie of the ground and the imbalance of forces, and seeing that all who faced the enemy must inevitably be left dead on the spot, yet judging it unworthy of his own virtue and magnanimity, and of the Lacedaemonian name, to fail in any part of his duty, he chose a middle course between those two extremes. He saved the youngest and fittest of his men for the service and defence of their country and sent them back; with the rest, whose loss would be of less moment, he resolved to hold the pass and, by their deaths, make the enemy pay as dearly as possible for getting through. And so it fell out: surrounded on all sides by the Arcadians, he and his men, after killing a great many of the enemy, were cut to pieces. Is there a single trophy dedicated to the conquerors that was not far more due to those who lost? The part of true conquering lies in the encounter, not in the coming out the other side; the honour of valour consists in fighting, not in subduing.

But to come back to my story: these prisoners are so far from showing the least weakness, in spite of all the terrors held up to them, that, on the contrary, during the two or three months they are kept they always wear a cheerful look, urge their captors to hurry up and put them to the test, defy them, jeer at them, taunt them with cowardice, and with the number of battles they have lost against their compatriots. I have a song made by one of these prisoners, in which he tells them to "come all and dine on him, and welcome, for in him they will also be eating their own fathers and grandfathers, whose flesh has gone to feed and nourish him. These muscles," he says, "this flesh and these veins, are your own: poor silly souls that you are, you little think that the substance of your ancestors' limbs is still here; pay attention to what you eat, and you will find in it the taste of your own flesh." In that song there is a touch of invention that has nothing barbarous about it. Those who paint these people dying in this manner show the prisoner spitting in the faces of his executioners and making wry mouths at them. And it is quite certain that to the very last gasp they never stop defying and braving them in word and gesture. In plain truth, these men are indeed savages compared with us; either they must be wholly so, or else we are; for there is a vast difference between their manners and ours.

The men there have several wives, and the more wives the higher their reputation for valour. And it is one very remarkable feature of their marriages that the same jealousy our wives use to keep us from the friendship and intimacy of other women, theirs use to further their husbands' desires and to procure them many partners. Above all things concerned for their husbands' honour, they make it their chief care to seek out and bring in as many companions as they can, since this is held to be evidence of their husband's worth. Most of our ladies will cry out that this is monstrous; in truth, it is not so, but a truly matrimonial virtue of the highest order. In the Bible, Sarah, with Leah and Rachel, the two wives of Jacob, gave the most beautiful of their handmaids to their husbands; Livia, in her own interest, indulged Augustus's passions for other women; and the wife of King Deiotarus, Stratonice, not only gave up a beautiful young maid in her service to her husband's embraces, but carefully brought up the children he had by her and helped them on to the succession of their father's crown.

And lest it be supposed that all this is done out of a simple, servile attachment to common custom, or by some authoritative impression of ancient practice, with no judgment or reasoning behind it — out of a soul too dull to think of anything else — I should give you a few touches of their understanding. Besides what I have just quoted of one of their war songs, I have another, a love song, that begins like this:

"Stay, adder, stay, so that by your pattern my sister may draw the design and work of a rich ribbon, which I may give to my beloved; and so your beauty and the exquisite order of your scales shall be preferred forever above all other serpents."

The first couplet — "Stay, adder," and so on — is the refrain of the song. Now I have spent enough time with poetry to be a judge of this much: that not only is there nothing barbarous in this invention, but it is, moreover, thoroughly Anacreontic. I might add that their language is soft, with a pleasing accent, and something close to Greek in its endings.

Three of these people, not foreseeing how dear a knowledge of the corruptions of this part of the world would one day cost their happiness and peace of mind — nor that their dealings with us are leading, as I take them to be, straight to their ruin (poor wretches, to let themselves be taken in by the desire for novelty, leaving the serenity of their own sky to come so far to gape at ours!) — were at Rouen when the late King Charles IX was there. The king himself talked with them a good while; they were shown our fashions, our pomp, the shape of a great city. Afterwards someone asked their opinion, wanting to know what among all the things they had seen they thought most worth admiring. To which they answered three things — of which I have forgotten the third, and am sorry for it, but two I still remember. They said, first, that they thought it very strange that so many tall men, bearded, strong, well-armed, who stood about the king (probably they meant the Swiss Guard), should submit to obeying a child, and not rather pick out one of their own number to command. Secondly (they have a way of speaking in their language by which they call men the halves of one another) they had noticed that there were among us men full and crammed with every sort of good, while their other halves were begging at their doors, lean and half-starved with hunger and poverty; and they thought it strange that these needy halves were able to bear such inequality and injustice, and did not take the others by the throat or set fire to their houses.

I talked with one of them for a good while, but I had so poor an interpreter, and one so muddled by his own ignorance to catch my meaning, that I could get nothing of much weight out of him. Asking what advantage he got from the rank he held among his own people (for he was a captain, and our sailors called him king), he told me: to march at the head of them to war. Asking him further how many men followed him, he showed me a stretch of ground to signify as many as could march on such a piece — perhaps four or five thousand men. Asking whether his authority lapsed with the war, he told me this much remained: that when he went to visit the villages under him, they cleared paths for him through the thick of the woods, so that he could pass at his ease. All this does not sound at all bad — and the last detail is not bad at all, considering they wear no breeches.

title: That a man is soberly to judge of the divine ordinances
paragraphs: The proper field and subject of imposture is the unknown — in the first place because the strangeness itself lends it credit, and besides, by not being subject to our ordinary reasoning, it deprives us of the means of questioning and arguing it. For this reason, Plato says, it is much easier to satisfy an audience when speaking of the nature of the gods than of the nature of men, because the listeners' ignorance opens a fair, wide road and gives every liberty in the handling of obscure things. From this it comes that nothing is so firmly believed as what we know least about, and no people are so confident as those who entertain us with fables — your alchemists, your judicial astrologers, fortune-tellers, and physicians —
"Id genus omne."
["All that sort of people." — Horace, Sat., i. 2, 2.]

To whom I would gladly add, if I dared, a pack of people who take upon themselves to interpret and supervise the designs of God himself, claiming to find the cause of every accident and to pry into the secrets of the divine will, in order to lay bare the incomprehensible motives of his works. And though the variety and the continual contradiction of events knock them from corner to corner, and toss them from east to west, they still keep up their futile inquisition, and with the same pencil paint both black and white.

Among one Indian nation there is a praiseworthy custom: when anything goes against them in some encounter or battle, they publicly ask pardon of the sun, who is their god, as though they had done some unjust act, always crediting their good or bad fortune to divine justice and submitting their own judgment and reason to it. It is enough for a Christian to believe that all things come from God, to receive them with acknowledgment of his divine and unsearchable wisdom, and so to accept them gratefully with whatever face they may wear. But I do not approve of the common practice of trying to confirm and support our religion by the success of our enterprises. Our belief has foundation enough without needing to be authorised by events. The people, accustomed to such plausible arguments, well-suited to their taste, are likely, when those arguments fail, to stagger in their faith too. So in this war we are now engaged in on account of religion, those who had the upper hand at the affair of Rochelabeille made loud boasts of it as an infallible approval of their cause, and then, when they had to excuse their misfortunes at Moncontour and Jarnac by calling them fatherly scourges and corrections — "because the people were not yet wholly at their mercy" — they show plainly enough what it is to draw two sorts of grist out of the same sack, and to blow hot and cold with the same mouth. It would be better to ground the common people in the solid, real foundations of truth. There was a fine naval battle won a few months ago under the command of Don John of Austria against the Turks; but it has also pleased God at other times to let us see victories just as great at our own expense. In short, it is a hard thing to reduce divine matters to our scales without losing a great deal of the weight in the spillage. And anyone who would try to give a reason why Arius and his Pope Leo, the principal heads of the Arian heresy, both died, at different times, of such similar and strange deaths (for, called away from disputation by a griping in the bowels, they both suddenly gave up the ghost on the privy), and would aggravate this divine vengeance by the circumstances of the place, might as well throw in the death of Heliogabalus, who was also killed in a privy. And Irenaeus, indeed, came to a similar end. God, pleased to show us that the good have something else to hope for, and the wicked something else to fear, than the fortunes or misfortunes of this world, manages and applies them according to his own hidden will and pleasure, and deprives us of the means of foolishly making a profit of them. So those people delude themselves who try to dive into these mysteries by the strength of human reason. They never strike one blow without taking two in return — of which St. Augustine makes a great proof against his opponents. It is a contest decided more by strength of memory than by force of reason. We must content ourselves with the light the sun is pleased to communicate to us by his rays; and whoever lifts up his eyes to take in more, let him not think it strange if, for the reward of his presumption, he loses his sight.
"Quis hominum potest scire consilium Dei? Aut quis poterit cogitare quid velit Dominus?"
["Who of men can know the counsel of God? or who can think what the will of the Lord is." — Book of Wisdom, ix. 13.]

title: That we are to avoid pleasures, even at the expense of life
paragraphs: I had long ago noticed that most of the ancients agreed on this: it is high time to die when there is more bad than good in living, and that to preserve life only for our own torment and discomfort runs against the very rules of nature, as these old maxims teach us.
["Either a tranquil life, or a happy death. It is good to die when life has become a burden. Better to die than to live in misery." — Stobaeus, Serm. xx.]

But to push contempt of death so far as to use it for clearing our minds of honours, riches, dignities, and the other gifts we call goods of fortune — as if reason alone were not enough to persuade us to give them up without this added injunction — I had never seen it commanded or practised until I came across this passage of Seneca. He was advising Lucilius, a man of great power and authority close to the emperor, to give up his lavish and pleasure-seeking way of life and retire to some quiet, solitary, philosophical existence. When Lucilius raised difficulties, Seneca said: "My opinion is that either you leave that life of yours, or life itself. I would advise the gentler way: untie, rather than break, the knot you have rashly tied. But if it cannot be untied otherwise, then break it cleanly. No man is so cowardly that he would not rather fall once than be always falling." I would have expected such counsel from Stoic severity, but it is stranger coming, as it does, from Epicurus, who writes the same thing on a similar occasion to Idomeneus. And I think I have noticed something like it — though with Christian moderation — among our own people.

St. Hilary, Bishop of Poitiers, that famous enemy of the Arian heresy, was in Syria when word reached him that Abra, his only daughter, whom he had left at home under her mother's care, was being sought in marriage by the greatest noblemen of the country — a virtuous, well-brought-up girl, beautiful, rich, and in the flower of her youth. He wrote back to her (as the record shows) that she should remove her affection from all the pleasures and advantages being offered, since on his travels he had found a far greater and worthier match for her: a husband of much greater power and magnificence, who would clothe her in robes and jewels of inestimable value. His aim was to wean her from the appetite for worldly delights and to join her wholly to God. And since the nearest and surest route to that, as he saw it, was his daughter's death, he never stopped praying and pleading with the Almighty to please call her out of this world and take her to himself. And it came to pass: soon after his return she died, at which he showed a singular joy. This seems to outdo the others, since he turns to this method from the start where they only resort to it secondarily, and it was on his own only daughter. But I will not leave out the rest of the story, even though it suits my purpose. St. Hilary's wife, learning from him how their daughter's death had been brought about by his deliberate prayer, and how much happier she was to be removed from this world than to have remained in it, conceived so vivid a sense of eternal and heavenly bliss that she begged her husband with utmost insistence to do the same for her. And God, at their joint request, soon called her too — a death embraced with singular and mutual contentment.

title: That fortune is oftentimes observed to act by the rule of reason
paragraphs: The inconstancy and various motions of Fortune

[The word Fortune, which Montaigne uses so often where he could have used Providence, was censured by the doctors who examined his Essays during his stay in Rome in 1581. See his Travels, i. 35 and 76.]

may reasonably make us expect her to show all sorts of faces. Can there be a clearer act of justice than this? The Duke of Valentinois, having resolved to poison Adrian, Cardinal of Corneto, with whom Pope Alexander VI — his father — and he himself were to dine in the Vatican, sent ahead a bottle of poisoned wine with strict orders to the butler to guard it well. The Pope arrived before his son and called for a drink. The butler, supposing the wine had been so carefully recommended only because of its quality, served it at once to the Pope. The duke himself came in soon after and, confident that no one had touched his bottle, also took a cup. So the father died on the spot, and the son, after long torment from illness, was reserved for another and a worse fortune.

Sometimes she seems to play with us in the very nick of an affair. Monsieur d'Estrees, then ensign to Monsieur de Vendome, and Monsieur de Licques, lieutenant in the Duc d'Ascot's company, were both rivals for the sister of the Sieur de Fougueselles, though on opposite sides — as often happens between frontier neighbours. The Sieur de Licques carried her off; but on the very day he was married, and worse, before he had gone to bed with his new wife, the bridegroom, eager to break a lance in honour of his bride, rode out to skirmish near St. Omer, where Sieur d'Estrees got the upper hand and took him prisoner. To make his victory more striking, the lady was forced —
"Conjugis ante coacta novi dimittere collum, Quam veniens una atque altera rursus hyems Noctibus in longis avidum saturasset amorem,"
["Compelled to release her arms from her new spouse's neck before two successive winters, in their long nights, had fed her eager love full." — Catullus, lxviii. 81.]
— to ask him as a favour to deliver up his prisoner to her, which he did. The gentlemen of France never refuse anything to a lady.

Doesn't she seem to play the artist here? Constantine, son of Helena, founded the empire of Constantinople, and many ages later, Constantine, son of Helen, brought it to its end. Sometimes she likes to mimic our miracles. We are told that when King Clovis was besieging Angoulême, the walls fell down on their own by divine favour; and Bouchet has it from some author that when King Robert was laying siege to a city and had slipped away from the siege to keep the feast of St. Aignan at Orleans, the walls of the besieged city collapsed in sudden ruin, without any assault, while he was at his devotions in a certain part of the Mass. But she did just the opposite in our Milan wars: Captain Rense was besieging Arona for us and had dug a mine under a great stretch of the wall; when the mine was sprung, the wall lifted off its foundations — and then dropped back down, whole and entire, exactly on its base, so that the besieged took no harm at all from the attempt.

Sometimes she plays the physician. Jason of Pheres, given up by the doctors because of an abscess in his chest, decided to rid himself of his pain at least by death, and threw himself recklessly into the thick of the enemy in a battle. He was so luckily wounded clean through the body that the abscess burst and he was completely cured. Did she not also outdo the painter Protogenes at his own art? He had finished a picture of a dog, panting and out of breath, well rendered in every other part but he could not get the foam and slaver coming from its mouth quite right. Furious with his work, he snatched up his sponge, which had soaked up various colours from cleaning his brushes, and hurled it at the picture meaning to ruin it. Fortune guided the sponge to land just at the dog's mouth, where it produced what all his skill could not. Does she not sometimes direct our plans and correct them? Isabel, Queen of England, sailing from Zealand back into her own kingdom with an army to support her son against her husband, would have been lost had she landed at the port she meant to, where the enemy lay in wait; but fortune, against her wishes, drove her into another harbour where she landed safely. And that man of old who, throwing a stone at a dog, hit and killed his mother-in-law — was he not right to declare:
["Fortune has more judgment than we do." — Menander]

Icetes had hired two soldiers to kill Timoleon at Adrana in Sicily. They picked their moment while he was at a sacrifice and pushed into the crowd. As they were signalling to each other that the time had come, a third man stepped in and felled one of them with a sword stroke across the head, leaving him dead on the spot, and ran off. The other, thinking himself discovered and as good as dead, fled to the altar and begged for mercy, promising to confess the whole plot. As he was doing so, laying out the full conspiracy, the third man — the one who had run — was caught and dragged through the crowd as a murderer, hauled before Timoleon and the chief men of the assembly. There he cried for pardon, pleading that he had justly killed his father's murderer. He proved it on the spot through reliable witnesses whom good fortune had conveniently provided — that his father had indeed been killed in the city of Leontini by the very man on whom he had now taken revenge. He was at once awarded ten Attic minae for having had the good fortune, by setting out to avenge his father's death, to preserve the life of the common father of Sicily. Fortune, truly, in her workings exceeds all the rules of human prudence.

To finish: is there not a clear show of her favour, generosity, and even piety in this episode? Ignatius the father and Ignatius the son, proscribed by the Roman triumvirs, agreed on the generous act of dying by each other's hands and so cheating the cruelty of the tyrants. Swords drawn, they rushed full tilt at one another, and fortune so guided the points that they each inflicted an equally mortal wound — while granting their brave friendship just enough strength left to draw out the bloody swords and embrace one another in their dying. They held each other so closely and so warmly that the executioner cut off both their heads at once, leaving the bodies still locked together in that noble bond, their wounds joined mouth to mouth, lovingly sucking in each other's last blood and life.
